The biggest risk to the thesis is cash conversion: H1 free cash flow was -₹11,585 cr (CFO/PAT -2.68×), likely because of gold inventory build and gold-loan funding, and together with high leverage this makes reported earnings look much weaker on a cash basis.

fundamental.thesis: Sundaram Finance is a conservatively run, mid-sized Chennai NBFC focused mainly on vehicle finance, with housing finance, asset management and a general-insurance JV (Royal Sundaram) under the group; it is known for steady growth and clean asset quality. H1FY27 consolidated PAT rose 20% to Rs 1,153 cr, and standalone Q2 PAT grew 21% to Rs 475 cr on 28% disbursement growth and 19% core AUM growth, with Gross Stage 3 improving to 1.84% from 2.03% and provision cover rising to 51% from 45%. However, momentum slowed within the half: consolidated PAT growth fell from +33.9% in Q1 to roughly +9% implied for Q2 (Rs 517 cr vs Rs 474 cr), and Q2 standalone profits from operations grew only 11%, partly because of a Rs 66 cr Supreme Court-driven motor third-party provision at Royal Sundaram. Using the lender yardstick of price-to-book against ROE, valuation looks fair to full: 3.5x book for a 16.75% ROE sits at P67 of peers on P/B and at P100 on forward P/E (21.2x vs a 14.6x median), so the quality premium is already priced in, and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut 1.4-1.8% over 90 days. The main risks are that this premium unwinds if the slower Q2 profit growth persists, and leadership transition after the chairman's resignation on 2026-11-05.

fundamental.thesis: Coforge is a fast-growing mid-tier Indian IT services firm focused on banking, insurance and travel clients, and it continues to out-grow tier-1 peers. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹6,171 cr (+53.6% YoY) with PAT of ₹588 cr (+56.5% YoY), quickening from +49.2% revenue growth in Q1 FY27; PAT margin held steady at about 9.5% and EBITDA margin rose slightly to 20.6%. The forward indicators also look strong: the 12-month executable order book is $2.38bn (+45% YoY), Q2 order intake was $1,040mn with 8 large deals signed, and guidance was raised. However, organic constant-currency growth was a much lower 5.2% QoQ in Q1, and the large AI-engineering and data service lines grew only +1.4% and -6.1% YoY, which suggests much of the headline growth is acquisition-led. On valuation, using P/E backed by EV/EBITDA and peer rank as the IT yardstick, trailing P/E of 32.95× is above the 22–30× sector range and at P88 vs peers. Forward P/E of 21.0× and EV/EBITDA of 15.8× (+7.6% vs the peer median, P67) are close to the peer median given roughly 50% growth, so the overall grade is fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that growth is mostly acquired rather than organic, with AI-driven deflation of legacy services underneath; a clear slowdown once the acquisition laps would hit the multiple.

fundamental.thesis: Ajanta Pharma is a branded-generics maker focused on chronic therapies: about 66% of revenue comes from branded generics across India (30%), Asia (18%) and Africa (18%), and US generics add 29%. In India it ranks #1 in ophthalmology and is the 4th fastest-growing of the top 25 companies, growing about 1.27x the Indian pharma market (16.7% vs 13.2%). Growth is speeding up. Revenue growth rose from +14% (Q2FY26) to +20% (Q3FY26) and +25% (Q1FY27), and reached about +32.5% in Q2FY27 (₹1,794 cr, implied from H1 ₹3,420 cr less Q1 ₹1,626 cr). Implied Q2 PAT of ₹388 cr is up about 49%, and PAT margin widened to about 21.6% from 19%, though cash conversion is only moderate (CFO/PAT 0.86x in H1). On the healthcare yardstick of trailing P/E plus peer rank, valuation is fair. Trailing P/E of 35.4x sits inside the 28-40x sector band and at P46 vs peers, and forward P/E of 26.3x signals expected earnings growth. EV/EBITDA of 24.3x (P69) and P/B of 8.3x (P77) carry a premium that a 25% ROE broadly justifies. The biggest risk is the 29% US generics exposure: generics are tariff-exempt for now, but the pending US Commerce review of generics plus forex losses already hitting reported profit could stall the margin gains, and management has given no forward guidance.

H1FY27 revenue grew +14.7% YoY to ₹2,367 cr, decelerating sharply from +28.8% in Q2FY26, while PAT grew only +5.1% YoY to ₹631 cr as PAT margin compressed from 39.0% (FY26) to 24.9% — the headline pain from a 25.7% YoY decline in Wealth Management segment PBT, partially offset by Asset Management revenue surging +65.7% YoY; ARR AUM for Wealth Management nonetheless grew +24.2% YoY, signalling the underlying fee base is intact even as near-term PBT is under pressure from rising employee costs (+28.7% YoY). On P/B plus ROE, the right yardstick for a lender, the stock looks cheap but not deeply so at 1.36x book with ROE of 11.6-12.7%, supported by a trailing P/E of 11.4x against the 18-28x NBFC range, though I give little weight to the broad-market peer rank because it has no true housing-finance peers and I disregard the 49% dividend yield as a data error. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹932 cr, up 20.5% YoY, a sharp turn from the -1.4% decline in FY26 (the yfinance figure of ₹592 cr does not match the official filing and is ignored), and management maintained its FY27 guidance of 18-20% revenue growth. Reported Q2 PAT of ₹164 cr (17.6% margin) includes a one-off ₹50 cr gain from the slump sale to the ACE KATO JV; without it the margin is about 11.65%, below Q1's 14.2% and FY26's 12.7%, so the 'expanding margin' signal mostly comes from that one-off while steel costs rose about 20%. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for an equipment maker, ACE trades at 20.7x against a broad-market median of 23.3x (P44), and its trailing P/E of 28.0x sits at the low end of the 28-45x industrials range (and is itself flattered by the one-off gain), so we grade it fair, not cheap. The biggest worry is cash: H1FY27 operating cash flow was roughly zero against ₹284 cr of PAT (CFO/PAT -0.03x, FCF -₹91 cr) because inventory jumped to ₹832 cr on defence order batching, and the order book of only ₹800-1,000 cr (about 0.25-0.28x revenue) gives limited forward visibility. Note also that the 21% dividend yield and 0.39 debt/equity in the snapshot look like data errors, since the filed debt/equity is 0.0.

fundamental.thesis: Great Eastern Shipping is India's largest private-sector shipping company, running crude and product tankers, LPG gas carriers (VLGCs) and dry-bulk ships, with an offshore-services arm. It is a cyclical freight-rate business, so the sector card's order-book framework for capital goods doesn't fit it well. The latest quarter, Q2 FY27, was the company's best ever. Revenue was ₹2,234 cr (+61.7% YoY) and net profit (PAT) was ₹1,269 cr (+118.4% YoY), a 56.8% PAT margin. That continues a sharp turnaround from shrinking revenue in H1 FY26 (-14.7%) to +66.9% in Q1 FY27 and +61.7% now. It was driven by Suezmax tanker earnings (+289% YoY to about $180,689/day) and VLGC earnings (+153% YoY). Earnings are cash-backed: operating cash flow is about 1.0x PAT, and the company holds ₹8,475 cr of net cash. For a cyclical, asset-heavy shipper the right yardstick is price-to-book against return on equity and the discount to net asset value (NAV), not P/E at a likely cyclical peak. On that basis it looks cheap: P/B is 1.19x with an 18.8% ROE, and management is buying back shares below NAV. Trailing P/E of 6.9x and EV/EBITDA of 4.7x sit in the bottom 5% of the market, though peak-cycle profits flatter both. The biggest risk is that freight rates fall back. Only about 58-61% of Q3 FY27 tanker and dry-bulk days are locked in, and forward P/E (7.2x) above trailing P/E suggests the market already expects earnings to fade, even though analysts have raised estimates by 26% over 90 days.

fundamental.thesis: Birlasoft is a mid-cap IT services company with about 11,100 staff, a shrinking base of 209 active clients and heavy reliance on its largest accounts (top 5 are 44.2% of revenue). Rupee revenue growth improved from -3.0% in H1 FY26 to +6.6% in Q2 FY27 and PAT rose 37.5% to about Rs 160 cr (11.3% margin; the table's Rs 142 cr revenue and Rs 16 cr PAT look like unit errors), but constant-currency revenue fell 1.6% and EBITDA margin slipped from 16.0% to 15.2%, so currency and possibly non-operating items appear to be flattering the headline trend. Using P/E and EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, the stock looks cheap at 13.8x trailing earnings against a 22-30x IT benchmark and at 6.1x EV/EBITDA, near its 52-week low, although the peer ranks are against the broad market rather than IT companies, and the 3.42 debt/equity and 231% dividend yield look like data errors and were not relied on. The biggest risk is that this is a value trap: H1 order wins rose 15% to $285M but Q2 new wins were only $47M, and falling client numbers plus AI price deflation could keep underlying growth negative.

fundamental.thesis: Zensar is an RPG-group mid-tier IT services firm with two businesses, Digital Services and Cloud Infrastructure, and it has a net cash position of ₹326 cr. Revenue is growing a little faster: H1FY27 revenue was ₹3,094 cr, up 10.2% YoY, compared with +7.5% to +8.7% through FY26, and Cloud Infrastructure grew 12.3%. Profit is not keeping up. H1 PAT of ₹374 cr rose only 2.7%, and PAT margin fell to 12.1% from 13.6% in FY26. Some of that drop is a one-off ₹24.9 cr Labour Code provision, but excluding it margin is still only about 12.9%. Cash conversion has also weakened, with CFO/PAT at 0.73x and only ₹22 cr of free cash flow because capex took up 8% of revenue, which is unusually high for an IT services firm. On valuation it looks cheap: trailing P/E is 12.6x against an IT sector band of 22–30x, EV/EBITDA is 8.2x (P7 across the market), and forward P/E of 11.2x is below trailing. Treat that discount with care, though. The stock is near its 52-week low, analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by about 1.2–1.4% over 90 days, and the market may be pricing in AI-driven shrinkage of mid-tier IT revenue. The feed also has several conflicting numbers: the Q1 revenue figure differs between sources, the Q2FY26 row is off by a factor of 10, and D/E of 1.68 and a 351% dividend yield contradict the net-cash position. So read the cheap grade with somewhat less confidence.

fundamental.thesis: ACME Solar is a renewable power producer with about 2,990 MW running and roughly 5,080 MW under construction, most of it solar, hybrid, firm-and-dispatchable (FDRE) and battery storage (BESS) projects. About 84% of its portfolio sells to central-government buyers on 25-year power purchase agreements (PPAs), and it signed a new 400 MW FDRE PPA with NTPC on 30 Oct. Growth is speeding up: revenue rose from +59% in FY26 to +63% in Q1 FY27 and +78% in H1 FY27, reaching ₹1,745 cr, while H1 PAT more than doubled (+105%) to ₹504 cr and PAT margin widened from 19.9% to 28.9%. Implied Q2 revenue was about ₹791 cr against ₹954 cr in Q1, which fits a weaker monsoon quarter for solar, so H1 is the cleaner read. I valued it on EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-heavy power producer. At 15.2x it sits around the 26th percentile of the broad market, and forward P/E of 13.7x versus trailing 40.7x shows strong earnings growth is already expected. On the other side, P/B of 4.0x with ROE of 10.4% is rich, and the stock is at 80% of its 52-week range, so I call it fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is the balance sheet: debt is about 3.9x equity, interest costs take about 40% of EBITDA, H1 free cash flow was negative ₹5,263 cr from heavy capex, and grid connection delays (about 6 months on average) could push back commissioning and the earnings it depends on.

fundamental.thesis: Castrol India is the market-leading branded lubricants company, with a 167,000-outlet distribution network that grew its rural reach to 46,000 outlets, so it behaves more like a consumer-brands business than the oil PSUs in the Energy sector card. For 9M CY26, revenue rose 20.3% YoY to ₹5,151 cr but PAT grew only 8.7% to ₹766 cr; backing out H1 (₹3,417 cr revenue, ₹590 cr PAT) implies the Sep-quarter revenue grew about 27% to roughly ₹1,734 cr while PAT fell about 22% to roughly ₹176 cr, so PAT margin dropped from 18.6% in the Jun quarter to about 10%, and the implied EBITDA margin of about 15% sits well below management's 21-24% target band. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E as the yardstick (not the PSU 'policy-priced' P/E-plus-yield framework), the stock trades at 17.7x trailing P/E and 11.9x EV/EBITDA, about 50% below the broad-market median (P18/P17), but trailing earnings include the stronger H1 and FY-EPS estimates were cut 4.9% over 30 days, so I grade it fair rather than cheap until margins stabilise. The biggest risk is that crude above $100 and a rupee at 95 per dollar keep raising base-oil costs faster than the company's low double-digit price hikes can pass them through, while weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.52x in H1) suggests working capital is soaking up the growth.

fundamental.thesis: MRPL is a standalone coastal refinery in Mangalore, majority-owned by ONGC. It earns on refining margins (GRM) plus a small, still loss-making retail fuel network, so its profits swing with the refining cycle. Q2 FY27 PAT was ₹1,881 cr, up 194% YoY from ₹639 cr. Implied Q2 revenue is about ₹35,590 cr (H1 ₹77,199 cr minus Q1 ₹41,609 cr), which works out to roughly +42% YoY by back-calculation. Growth is still very strong but has slowed from +98% in Q1. Profitability actually improved: the PAT margin rose from 2.5% in Q1 to about 5.3% in Q2, and H1 earnings were well backed by cash (CFO/PAT 2.1x). Note that the pre-computed 'accelerating revenue / contracting margin' labels appear to read the table in the wrong order. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive refiner. At 6.0x it sits at P3 vs the broad market, but trailing P/E of 14.5x is above the 6–10x norm the sector card sets for PSU refiners and OMCs. The 3.4x forward P/E looks unreliable because next-year EPS estimates were cut 21% in 30 days. Taken together, I grade the stock 'fair' and priced for peak margins rather than cheap. The biggest risk is that this is peak-cycle earnings: geopolitically inflated cracks could normalise while freight stays elevated at $7–10/bbl, and the Coker Hydrotreater fire keeps that unit offline until mid-December.

fundamental.thesis: Oil India is a state-owned upstream oil and gas producer, with a refining arm through its stake in Numaligarh Refinery (NRL), so its earnings rise and fall with crude prices. The trend data does not add up: Q1 FY27 showed revenue of ₹12,886 cr (+47.3% YoY) and PAT of ₹4,027 cr (+96.9%), but the H1 FY27 row shows only ₹11,915 cr revenue (-33.5%) and ₹2,520 cr PAT (-31.7%), which is smaller than Q1 alone and conflicts with the company's own press release of 116% standalone PAT growth in Q2 on 20% higher crude output, so the H1 row is probably a mix of standalone and consolidated figures and I have not used it as the latest quarter. On the sector card's yardstick for PSU upstream (P/E of 6–10× plus dividend yield, with EV/EBITDA as a check), a trailing P/E of 10.3× sits at the top of that band and inside the 8–14× energy median, EV/EBITDA is 8.3× and P/B is 1.18× against a 12.7% ROE, so I grade it fair (priced for policy risk) rather than cheap. The forward P/E of 6.9× and sell-side EPS estimates raised 15% in 30 days support the near-term earnings outlook, but the 'cheap vs peers' verdict is against the whole market rather than true peers and should not be relied on. Crude is now falling, which the macro desk scores as a strong headwind for upstream producers, and Energy is underweight.

fundamental.thesis: Bharti Hexacom is Bharti Airtel's listed subsidiary covering the Rajasthan and North-East telecom circles, with about 30 million customers. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹2,582 cr, up 11.4% YoY, a slight pick-up from 10.9% in Q1 and 9.4% for FY26. PAT was ₹566 cr, up 34.4%, with PAT margin widening to 21.9% from 19.2% in Q1. EBITDAaL rose 14.2%, cash generation is strong (FY26 CFO/PAT of 2.6x) and net debt is low at 0.31x EBITDAaL. The weak spot is ARPU, the sector's key number: it grew only 5.2% to ₹264, which suggests growth is coming more from data usage and broadband than from pricing power. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick the sector card names. At 15.4x it is well above the 9-12x norm for Indian mobile, and a trailing P/E of 41x is also expensive. A forward P/E of 22x already assumes a lot of earnings growth, while analysts have cut EPS estimates 2-3% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that the next tariff hike gets delayed while estimates keep falling, which could push the multiple down even with the stock near its 52-week low.

The technical view is hold because the stock is up about 14% in a month and is extended, not pulling back to support near 1317. The regime penalises late entries, Energy is underweight, and crude plus the rupee are a net headwind (-2). With only about ₹10k of cash (around 7 shares) and no weakened holding identified to trim, a token position isn't worth it. Better to wait for a pullback toward 1317-1330 and re-check then.

fundamental.thesis: Reliance is India's largest conglomerate and should be read as four businesses: refining and petrochemicals (O2C), Jio telecom (JPL, now separately listed after its 28 Oct 2026 IPO), retail (RRVL) and a new-energy build-out. Q2FY27 revenue rose 27.8% YoY to ₹362,268 cr, up from +24.5% in Q1 and -8.5% in FY26, and PAT rose 33.8% to ₹29,550 cr, a margin of 8.2% (up from 6.8% in Q1, roughly flat against FY26's 8.3%). Most of that came from O2C, where EBITDA jumped 67.9% to ₹25,203 cr on fuel cracks 3–3.7x higher after Middle East supply disruptions; Jio grew steadily (revenue +11.4%, ARPU ₹218.8), but retail PAT fell 24.3% and JioStar PAT fell 13.2%. Using a sum-of-the-parts view with EV/EBITDA as the main multiple, the stock trades at 12.2x EV/EBITDA and 21.7x trailing / 18.0x forward P/E; that looks expensive against the PSU energy median (9.2x P/E), but that comparison is misleading for a conglomerate earning telecom and retail multiples, so I grade it fair. It trades near its 52-week low, has strong cash conversion (CFO/PAT 1.76x) and modest leverage (net debt/EBITDA 0.47x). The biggest risk is that the record quarter depends on crack spreads created by a geopolitical shock, which can reverse quickly while retail and media are weakening.

fundamental.thesis: NTPC is India's largest power generator. Most of its earnings come from a regulated return (about 15.5% ROE) on the plants it has commissioned, with a fast-growing solar and renewables arm on top. H1 FY27 headline revenue was ₹100,262 cr, up 19.9% from ₹83,660 cr a year ago, but the company's core capacity-plus-energy billing grew a more modest 9.65%. Within that, capacity charges rose 6.7% to ₹35,909 cr, energy charges rose 11.6% to ₹55,845 cr and solar revenue rose 64.9% to ₹2,456 cr. Revenue growth has turned up from about -1.5% to -3% in FY26 to +7.0% in Q1 FY27 (PAT ₹6,896 cr, +12.9%, 13.6% margin), though H1 PAT was not extracted. For a capital-intensive utility I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, backed by P/B with ROE. On that basis it looks cheap against peers: EV/EBITDA is 8.4x against a peer median of 11.6x (cheapest in the peer group) and trailing P/E is 11.9x against 14.7x. P/B is 1.7x with ROE of 13.7%. It is only fair against the static 10–18x utilities P/E band. The forward P/E (12.8x) is above the trailing P/E, and this year's EPS estimates were trimmed 0.9% in the last 30 days, so near-term earnings look roughly flat. The main risk is earnings quality: CERC 2024 tariff orders are still pending, so bills are provisional and later adjusted (₹2,825 cr energy adjustment in H1), and large regulatory-deferral and deferred-tax swings make reported PAT hard to compare across periods.

fundamental.thesis: Nestle India is a leading packaged-food company (MAGGI, NESCAFE, KITKAT, infant nutrition) with deep rural and urban distribution and a premium brand franchise. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 20.5% YoY to ₹6,782 cr and PAT rose 36.3% to ₹1,027 cr (15.1% PAT margin), with double-digit volume growth reported across all product groups. Growth is slowing slightly from Q1FY27, when revenue grew 25.4% and PAT 47.9%. EBITDA margin dipped slightly to 23.8% from 24.2%, and ad spend rose 46%, so margins are not being protected by cutting brand investment. On the P/E yardstick for FMCG staples, trailing P/E of 77x sits above the sector norm of 40-65x and above the peer median of 51.5x (P83), and forward P/E of 59x is the most expensive in the sector (P100), so the stock is expensive. The biggest risk is a valuation de-rating: the current 11% volume growth is far above the company's 5-year volume CAGR of 4.2%, and the price assumes it lasts while cocoa and milk costs keep pressing on margins.

fundamental.thesis: JSW Steel is a large Indian steelmaker that sold a record 7.46 MT in Q2FY27 (+13% YoY), with auto-sector sales up 36%. Revenue growth accelerated from +9.8% in Q1 to +20.6% (₹54,486 cr), and PAT rose 225.6% to ₹5,359 cr, though the YoY figures use a low, restructured base; PAT margin was flat at about 9.8-9.9%, the 'contracting' signal is distorted by FY26's ₹18,051 cr one-off gain, and EBITDA per tonne fell about 11% QoQ from ₹14,990 to ₹13,329 despite rising 24% YoY. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a steel cyclical, the stock is expensive: the reported 12.6x, or roughly 9x on my estimate using annualised Q2 EBITDA and net debt, is above the 5-8x mid-cycle norm, and the 13.8x trailing P/E and 'cheap vs peers' verdict carry little weight because of the one-off gain and a peer set that includes paint and adhesive companies. The biggest risk is that steel spreads narrow from here, with the stock at 92% of its 52-week range and EBITDA per tonne already falling sequentially, leaving little room for error.

fundamental.thesis: Bajaj Auto is one of India's largest two- and three-wheeler makers and a leading exporter, with a fast-growing electric line (Chetak at about 23.5% e-2W share) and a growing finance arm (BACL). In Q2 FY27 it reported revenue of ₹20,003 cr and PAT of ₹3,354 cr, a PAT margin of 16.8%, up from 14.9% in Q1 FY27, with EBITDA margin flat at 20.9%. Clean revenue growth versus last year cannot be calculated because the filed figures appear to include the newly consolidated KTM parent (Bajaj Mobility) and the finance arm, while yfinance shows ₹16,834 cr. Volumes are the cleaner signal: total volumes rose 20% YoY, driven by exports up 41%, while domestic volumes grew only 4%. On EV/EBITDA, the multiple suited to a capital-intensive maker, the stock trades at 19.8x against a peer median of 18.3x, with a trailing P/E of 26.6x (P40 among peers, inside the 18–30x OEM range) and a forward P/E of 22.0x; that makes it fair, not cheap, especially at 85% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is management's own warning that steel and copper inflation could cost about 2% of revenue in Q3–Q4, with October price hikes recovering only about 30% of it, at a time when growth is leaning on exports rather than the home market.

fundamental.thesis: SBI Life is a large listed Indian life insurer with a market cap of about ₹1.8L cr, and the sector card says to judge it on new business value (VNB), APE growth and price-to-embedded-value (P/EV), not PAT. H1 FY27 shows embedded value of ₹87,350 cr and six-month VNB of ₹3,270 cr, but no reliable growth rate can be calculated because the year-ago figures (₹7,600 cr and ₹275 cr) look like unit errors; the last usable revenue and PAT growth is Q1 FY27 at +16.9% and +21.9%, revenue growth has stayed in a +16% to +19% range rather than clearly slowing as the trend signal says, and the table mixes quarterly and cumulative periods. On P/EV, the stock trades at about 2.1x (₹1.8L cr / ₹87,350 cr), which I grade fair on a provisional basis because no peer or historical P/EV is provided; the 71.7x trailing P/E (peer median 53.7x) is not the right yardstick, and the 15% of 52-week range position offers a better entry only if growth holds, while the 15.0% dividend yield looks like a data error and is ignored. The main concern is business quality: 13-month persistency has slipped from 87.11% in H1 FY26 to 84.35% in Q1 FY27 and the expense ratio has risen from 10.9% to 12.05%, while FY EPS estimates have edged down about 1% over 90 days despite 34 of 35 analysts rating it a buy.

fundamental.thesis: Eicher Motors owns Royal Enfield, which has about 84% of India's mid-size motorcycle segment, so the company rides the shift to premium bikes, with VECV trucks as a smaller second business. Half-year revenue was ₹14,054 cr (+25.3% YoY) and PAT ₹3,036 cr (+17.9%), but taking H1 minus Q1 puts Q2 FY27 at about ₹7,422 cr revenue (around +20% YoY) and ₹1,573 cr PAT (around +15%). That is a slowdown from Q1's +31.6% revenue and +21.4% PAT, and PAT margin has slipped from 23.6% in FY26 to about 21.2%, even though cash conversion is strong (1.21x CFO/PAT, essentially no net debt). On the auto-OEM P/E yardstick from the sector card (18–30x), the trailing P/E of 37.9x is above the band and the forward P/E of 28.8x sits at the top of it; the stock is also at P80–P100 against auto peers on every multiple (EV/EBITDA 33.7x vs a 18.3x median) and at 79% of its 52-week range, so it grades expensive despite best-in-class quality. The main risk is that profit growth keeps lagging revenue growth while the stock trades at a premium multiple, which leaves little room for a softer post-festive demand print or a stumble in the J1 engine platform switch.

fundamental.thesis: Pidilite is India's dominant adhesives and sealants franchise (Fevicol, Dr. Fixit) and earns consumer-brand economics, so it should be valued against the 30–60× P/E range for consumer franchises, not against the steel and chemical cyclicals in its sector peer set. The latest quarter with numbers is Q1FY27: revenue was ₹4,552 cr (+21.3% YoY) and PAT ₹884 cr (+29.8% YoY). PAT margin was 19.4%, up from 16.8% for FY26, and EBITDA margin was 28.6%, up from 25.9% for FY26. However, the Q2FY27 and H1FY27 results filed on 2026-10-28 were not extracted, so the most recent quarter is missing, and the Q3FY26 row (₹996 cr, +53%) looks wrong, which makes the 'decelerating' growth signal unreliable. On the consumer-franchise yardstick the stock is fair but at the rich end: trailing P/E is 57.1×, near the top of the 30–60× range, while forward P/E of 46.8× and EV/EBITDA of 39.9× already assume continued double-digit earnings growth. The price sits mid-way in its 52-week range and the mean analyst target is only about 5% above it. The P93–P100 peer ranks mostly reflect the cyclical comparison set and are not a clean signal. The biggest risk is that a premium multiple meets a Q2 we have not seen, with crude-linked input costs (VAM) rising and full-year EPS estimates cut 1.7% over the last 30 days.

The biggest risk is that Q1 was a lumpy peak quarter; if Q2 results on 7 Nov show margins normalising toward guidance, a multiple this rich leaves little room for disappointment.

fundamental.thesis: Godrej Properties is an asset-light residential developer that has doubled its national market share from 2.4% in CY21 to 4.8% in CY25. Its FY26 operating base looks healthy: bookings were ₹34,171 cr (+16% YoY), collections ₹19,965 cr (+17%) and new project additions ₹42,100 cr (+59%). Reported H1 FY27 numbers are weaker: revenue rose 107.8% YoY to ₹2,441 cr, but PAT fell 49.8% to ₹495 cr (12.6% margin). That PAT includes a ₹309 cr non-cash fair-value gain, so underlying profit is roughly ₹186 cr. Operating cash flow was negative at ₹-724 cr, and net debt rose from ₹7,607 cr in Q1 to ₹8,111 cr. The trend table mixes quarterly, half-year and full-year periods, so the 'accelerating' and 'contracting' labels are not reliable, and H1 FY27 bookings and collections are not in the data, which leaves a gap in the metrics that matter most here. I graded valuation on enterprise value to pre-sales (bookings) and P/B against ROE, not P/E, because reported profit here lags actual sales by 2–4 years. Enterprise value is about ₹59,500 cr, or roughly 1.7× FY26 bookings. P/B is 2.68× against ROE of 10%, and the stock sits at 25% of its 52-week range, so it looks fair, leaning slightly cheap. The biggest risk is that cash generation weakens while debt rises in a risk-off market.

fundamental.thesis: Nuvama is a wealth management and capital markets firm (private wealth, broking, asset services and asset management). It is a fee and market-linked business, not a lender, so this is a cyclical, market-beta franchise. In the latest extracted quarter (Q1FY27) consolidated PAT rose 38.0% YoY to ₹305.64 cr from ₹221.48 cr at a steady 22.1% margin. That growth is low quality: capital markets revenue fell 15.6% YoY to ₹172.09 cr, ₹250.17 cr came from holding-company investment income, revenue growth fell from +107% in FY25 to -12.5% in FY26, and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-06 are not yet in the extracted data. On valuation I used P/B against ROE plus P/E, since AUM-linked earnings data is unavailable: P/B of 7.6x is backed by a 27.3% ROE, and the trailing P/E of 30.6x (forward 21.6x) sits near the broad-market median at P43. That makes it fair, not cheap, especially with the stock at 91% of its 52-week range and FY EPS estimates cut 1.9% over 30 days. The biggest risk is that earnings lean on investment income and market activity while the core capital markets line shrinks, and a fresh promoter encumbrance disclosure (2026-11-04) adds a governance flag for a midcap.

fundamental.thesis: Delhivery is India's largest independent third-party logistics company, earning most of its revenue from e-commerce express parcels and part-truckload (PTL) freight. It does not run on an order book, so the card's order-book yardstick does not fit and it is judged here on volume growth, margins and EV/EBITDA. Q2 FY27 revenue was ₹3,066 cr, up 20.0% YoY, a slowdown from +27.8% in Q1 (the pre-computed 'accelerating' label reads this backwards). EBITDA margin fell from 8.6% to 6.7% quarter-on-quarter, and PAT was only ₹41 cr, a 1.3% margin, after Q1 PAT dropped 65% YoY. Parcel volumes grew 32% but parcel revenue only 22%, so the company is earning less per shipment; PTL is healthier, with tonnage up 14% and revenue up 23%. On valuation, EV/EBITDA of 111x (P98 vs the market) and trailing P/E of 231x make it expensive even after the cash cushion of about ₹4,676 cr. Forward P/E of 41x still assumes a big profit ramp that analysts are cutting: FY EPS estimates are down 14% in 30 days and 26% in 90 days, while 18 of 20 ratings stay at buy. That gap is a classic setup for the stock to re-rate lower.

fundamental.thesis: Gujarat Fluorochemicals is a major Indian maker of fluoropolymers and fluorochemicals; its chemicals arm brings in about 98% of revenue, and it is also building a battery-materials (EV) business that is still at an early stage. fundamental.thesis: NATCO Pharma is a mid-cap specialty generics maker whose profits have depended heavily on limited-competition US launches, especially generic Revlimid (lenalidomide). It also has a smaller domestic formulations business, an API business and a crop-health business. In Q2 FY27, revenue fell 30.4% YoY to ₹1,019cr and PAT fell 60.9% to ₹203cr. The PAT margin dropped to 19.9% from 34.8% in FY26 and 42.6% in FY25, mainly because International Formulations fell 41.4% as the lenalidomide windfall wears off. There are some offsets: domestic pharma grew 38%, API 14%, crop health 16%, and revenue rose 28% from Q1. I graded valuation mainly on forward P/E and EV/EBITDA, because the trailing P/E of 11.2× still includes one-off Revlimid profits that will not repeat. The forward P/E of 19.3× is higher than the trailing figure, which means earnings are expected to fall further. Even so, 19.3× forward and 9.6× EV/EBITDA are below the 28–40× pharma range, and P/B is 1.8× against ROE of 16.9%, so the stock is cheap on paper. I grade it fair rather than cheap because the earnings base is still shrinking and the replacement pipeline has not yet shown it can fill the gap. The biggest risk is that this is a value trap: cash conversion is weak, the company needed a ₹750/share rights issue, and the 49% stake in Adcock Ingram adds acquisition-integration risk while the core US earnings keep fading.

fundamental.thesis: Hindustan Zinc is India's dominant integrated zinc-lead-silver miner (Vedanta Group subsidiary) with near-monopoly status in domestic mined zinc and structural cost advantages that produce world-class EBITDA margins of 62.4% — a level no domestic peer can match. H1FY27 revenue surged 76.7% YoY to ₹28,840 cr (accelerating sharply from -4.4% in Q1FY26), PAT grew 143.4% YoY to ₹11,881 cr, and PAT margin expanded to 41.2% from 29.9% — a five-period trajectory of simultaneously accelerating revenue growth and expanding margins driven primarily by elevated zinc and silver commodity prices, with cash quality strong (CFO/PAT 1.12×). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive commodity miner, the stock trades at 10.59× — P13 among 473 peers and a 54.6% discount to the broad-market EV/EBITDA median — with trailing P/E of 17.46× squarely inside the Materials sector range (12–22×), grading cheap on peer-relative metrics, though 10.59× sits above the 5–8× typical mid-cycle range for base-metals cyclicals, signalling that some commodity-cycle-peak risk remains unpriced. The thesis is materially constrained by an unresolved ED/FEMA investigation (search and seizure June 2026, no regulatory communication as of the October 2026 filing) and SEBI observations on related party transaction disclosures — governance headwinds typical of Vedanta Group that can trigger a de-rating independent of commodity fundamentals, and are weighted heavily under the midcap governance overlay.

fundamental.thesis: Abbott India is the Indian listed arm of Abbott. It is a branded-formulations franchise focused on the domestic market (Thyronorm, Duphaston and other women's health, gastro and chronic-therapy brands), so it is in the sector card's 'safe template' group with no US-tariff exposure. The only reliable figures are full-year FY26: revenue of ₹6,929 cr (+8.1% YoY) and PAT of ₹1,552 cr (+9.7% YoY), with a 27.7% EBITDA margin and a stable 22.4% PAT margin. Cash conversion was good but not excellent (CFO/PAT 0.85x, FCF ₹1,278 cr). The Q1FY27 yfinance row does not add up (₹932 cr revenue against a ~₹1,730 cr quarterly run-rate, and a 46% PAT margin), so I ignored it. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-05 have not been extracted yet, which means I cannot read the current trend. On valuation, the trailing P/E of 35.8x sits inside the 28-40x pharma range and at P52 against peers, and EV/EBITDA is 28.1x (P62), so I grade it fair. The forward P/E of 28.8x points to expected earnings growth, and the stock trades at 8.4% of its 52-week range, a better entry point if the Q2 numbers hold up. The biggest risk is that the price slide reflects a weaker Q2 or growth slowing to mid-single digits, which this stale data cannot confirm or rule out. Two of the snapshot figures are almost certainly data errors and I ignored them: a dividend yield of 201% and debt/equity of 3.6 for a company that has historically had no debt (the second may be lease liabilities or a unit mismatch).

fundamental.thesis: KIMS is a multi-specialty hospital chain anchored in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, now in a heavy expansion phase into new cities (it has signed an O&M deal for Westfort Hospital, Thrissur, and is merging a subsidiary into the parent); its growth comes from new beds plus occupancy and revenue-per-bed gains. In the latest officially extracted quarter (Q1 FY27), consolidated revenue rose 35.3% YoY to ₹1,180 cr, keeping a run of +28-35% top-line growth, but PAT fell 56.5% to ₹37 cr, and margins have shrunk steadily (EBITDA margin 21.1% in FY26 to 18.8%, PAT margin 6.2% to 3.1%) as new hospitals carry start-up losses, depreciation and interest. Q2 FY27 results were filed on 2026-11-04 but are not yet in the extracted trend table, and the yfinance quarterly rows (₹457-510 cr revenue) do not match the consolidated PDF scale, so I have not relied on them. On valuation, using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for a capital-heavy hospital operator, 44.5x sits at P85 of the broad market (+91% vs the 23.3x median), and trailing P/E of 131.6x, P/B of 14.1x against ROE of only 9.7%, and a price at 91% of the 52-week range all point to expensive. The forward P/E of 46x assumes a sharp profit recovery that analysts are actively cutting (FY EPS estimates down 14% over 30 and 90 days), so the main risk is that slow ramp-up of new hospitals, on a highly leveraged balance sheet, delays the margin recovery the price already assumes.

Chalet Hotels is a midcap owner-operator of upscale and luxury hotels, mainly in Mumbai, plus commercial office rentals (CIGNUS) and a residential project. Its results are distorted by timing. Reported Q2FY27 revenue was ₹511 cr, down 31.2% YoY, because the large FY26 residential handover did not repeat. Core hotel and rental revenue grew about 11% YoY, with EBITDA up 13% and margin up 110 bps to roughly 45%. RevPAR rose 7.2% to ₹8,702, driven by ADR (+11.3%), while occupancy fell 244 bps to 64.2%; MMR occupancy dropped 667 bps on West Asia and air-travel disruption. Reported PAT of ₹216 cr (+39.7%, a 42.3% margin) is inflated by a one-off deferred tax credit from switching to the lower tax regime, so the underlying margin is lower and should not be read as a trend. On EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive hotel owner, the stock trades at 15.7×, about 33% below the broad-market median (P27), with trailing P/E at 26.4× and the price at 22% of its 52-week range. That makes it fair, leaning cheap, but the peer set is broad-market rather than hotel peers. The main risk is the capex push: ₹3,400–3,600 cr over FY27–FY29 has already lifted net debt to ₹2,113 cr while occupancy is softening.

H1 FY27 PAT was Rs 320 cr vs Rs 106 cr in the H1 FY26 row (about +202%, not the +526% shown), and implied Q2 PAT of about Rs 264 cr matches yfinance's Rs 263 cr, but the growth trend is unreliable: H1 revenue of Rs 2,717 cr (shown as -21.2%) is -17.5% against Rs 3,292 cr, its 8.4% PAT margin implies about Rs 3,800 cr (+16%), and the 'decelerating revenue' and 'expanding margin' signals mix H1 and quarterly rows, with Q1 FY26 revenue of Rs 147 cr looking like a 10x error, so Q1 FY27's +11.9% is the last usable growth figure. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive, lease-heavy business, 7.41x (P6 vs a broad-market peer set, not cinema peers) with P/B of 1.27x and a price at 14% of the 52-week range grades cheap, with modest confidence because the 53.06x trailing P/E appears to exclude H1 FY27 profit, the 16.16x forward P/E needs earnings to roughly triple, ROE is only 2.4%, and the consensus '+7.7% upside' implies a price near Rs 1,524, well above the Rs 1,250 52-week high. The biggest risks are that a weak film slate hits a high fixed-cost business and that the recovery proves less durable than the +27.6% estimate upgrades suggest; separately, the promoter's Regulation 31 disclosure dated 2026-11-03 needs checking for any share pledge, and no footfall, ticket-price or management guidance data was available.

fundamental.thesis: Amara Raja Energy & Mobility is India's second-largest lead-acid battery maker (Amaron) and is building a lithium-ion cell and pack business. On EV/EBITDA, the yardstick we use for this capital-heavy business, the stock trades at 10.3x, cheaper than about 89% of the broad market, and its trailing P/E of 17.4x sits just below the 18-28x auto-ancillary range. That makes it cheap on paper, but sell-side FY EPS estimates were cut about 10% in the last 30 days, so the cheapness is partly a falling-earnings effect. The biggest risk is that lead-acid margins keep shrinking while the loss-making new-energy unit (Rs 64 cr H1 loss) and Rs 2,320 cr of new LFP capex keep free cash flow negative (Rs -161 cr in H1).

fundamental.thesis: CIE Automotive India makes forged, cast and machined components for auto OEMs, with about two-thirds of revenue from India and the rest from Europe (it reports on a calendar year, so 9M26 means Jan–Sep 2026). Revenue for 9M26 rose 12.1% YoY to ₹7,866 cr and PAT rose 16.8% to ₹729 cr. India grew 14.7% while Europe grew only 7.4%. Growth is steady but edging down: from +13.0% in H1 to +12.1% for 9M, which implies about +10% in Q3 on its own. EBITDA margin also slipped from 16.7% in H1 to 16.1% for 9M. I graded valuation on P/E, the yardstick the sector card uses for auto names. Trailing P/E is 20.0x, in the lower half of the sector's 18–30x band, and forward P/E is 15.9x, so the market expects earnings to grow. EV/EBITDA is 18.9x against a broad-market median of 23.3x. That makes the stock fair, leaning cheap, but the peer ranking (P22 on P/E) compares it with the whole market, not auto peers, so I put less weight on it. The main risks are weak cash conversion (H1 free cash flow was -₹263 cr, with operating cash flow at -0.04x PAT) and a slow Europe business. Analysts keep cutting estimates (FY EPS down 2.3% over 90 days) even though 4 of 5 rate it a buy, and rising crude in a risk-off market is a headwind for auto demand.

fundamental.thesis: UNO Minda makes auto components for Indian OEMs, including lighting, switches, alloy wheels, acoustics, sunroofs and EV parts. It is a domestic-focused ancillary that benefits from premiumisation and the shift to EVs, and it announced a sunroof capacity expansion with its results. The Q2 press release reports record growth of 38% YoY in both revenue and PAT, so momentum is speeding up from the roughly 18-20% growth seen in FY26 and Q3 FY26. Cash backing is good: FY26 operating cash flow was 1.44x PAT. The quarter-by-quarter split in the trend table does not add up, though (the Q1 row of ₹5,557 cr cannot be reconciled with H1), and EBITDA margin slipped from 12.6% to 11.2%. Valuation is expensive: P/E is 53x trailing and 35.5x forward against an Auto-ancillary median of 18-28x, EV/EBITDA is 29x and P/B is 10x on a 19% ROE. All of these sit at the 64th-82nd percentile of the broad market, and the mean analyst target is only 2.4% above the price, even though analysts have raised EPS estimates by about 6% over the past 90 days. The main risk is that minority shareholders in subsidiaries take a growing share of profit: EPS grew only 3.6% against 19.7% PAT growth, which leaves little room for any slowdown after the festive season at this multiple.

fundamental.thesis: ZF Commercial Vehicle Control Systems India supplies braking, air-management and transmission (AMT) systems to commercial vehicle makers in India and abroad. It is the only OEM supplier of e-compressors for electric buses, and an e-bus kit is worth about 5x a standard truck kit (roughly ₹2.25-2.5 lakh vs ₹45,000). Sales are speeding up but profits are not keeping pace: H1 FY27 revenue rose 20.8% YoY to ₹2,281 cr, up from +0.8% to +3.1% a year ago. The implied Q2 FY27 (H1 minus Q1) is about ₹1,215 cr in revenue (+27% YoY) and ₹130 cr in PAT (+20%), yet H1 PAT grew only 1.6%, and the EBITDA margin fell from 22.9% in Q2 FY26 to 16.6% in H1 FY27. Cash generation is still solid: H1 CFO/PAT was 1.04x, free cash flow ₹203 cr, and the company holds net cash. On valuation, the 2.83x trailing P/E and 16% dividend yield in the snapshot are clearly broken, most likely because the 5:1 bonus was not adjusted for. SJVN is a government-owned power generator, historically a hydro-heavy regulated utility, now adding thermal capacity (the 1320 MW Buxar plant's second unit was just dedicated) and pursuing new hydro projects such as the 669 MW Lower Arun project in Nepal. The implied Q2FY27 figures (H1 minus Q1) are about ₹2,245 cr revenue (+117% YoY) and ₹657 cr PAT (+113%), but they include ₹283 cr of catch-up tariff from CERC orders, and EBITDA margin has fallen from about 86% to about 48% as lower-margin thermal enters the mix. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, 15.9x is about 32% below the broad-market median but rich for a regulated generator. Trailing P/E of 38x is far above the 10–18x utilities range, while forward P/E of 14x sits inside it, and P/B of 1.86x is near the 52-week low, so the overall grade is fair rather than cheap. The biggest risk is the stretched balance sheet: debt/equity is 2.25x, debt-service coverage is 0.6x, and the current ratio is 0.54. On top of that, the Etalin project has been reassigned, Devasari is on indefinite hold, and next-FY EPS estimates have been cut 18.7% in 30 days, so the earnings jump may not persist once one-offs drop out.

On the appropriate lender yardstick (P/B + ROE), IIFL trades at 1.62× P/B with a 12.3% ROE — borderline cheap — confirmed by a P11 broad-market percentile rank on trailing P/E and a forward P/E of 7.66× (vs trailing 13.65×) that implies strong consensus earnings growth priced in at a meaningful discount to NBFC sector median of 18–28×. The biggest fundamental risk is governance: the re-designation of co-founder R Venkataraman from Joint MD to Non-Executive Director on October 15 is a leadership change at a sensitive recovery juncture, compounded by a declining Provision Coverage Ratio (114% in Q3FY25 to 63% in H1FY26) and deeply negative cash conversion (CFO/PAT −7.34×), all of which limit conviction despite the appealing valuation.

fundamental.thesis: Union Bank of India is a large public-sector lender, and its asset quality and loan growth are clearly getting better. In Q2 FY27, total income rose only +3.2% YoY to ₹32,809 cr, but PAT jumped +29.9% to ₹5,537 cr, pushing the PAT margin up to 16.9% from 13.4% a year ago. Under the hood the trend is clean: NIM rose from 2.67% to 2.86% over four quarters, gross NPA fell from 3.29% to 2.42%, net NPA fell to 0.42%, credit cost is low at 0.21%, and loan growth sped up from about 5% to about 13% YoY. Using the P/B-plus-ROE yardstick for lenders (P/E is ignored for banks), the stock trades at 1.01× book against a 15.7% TTM ROE (17.2% in Q2), so it is cheap. That reading is backed by a bottom-3rd-percentile rank on P/B. The main caution is that profits are rising much faster than income, which leans on low provisions and margin gains that may not last as rates reset, and 164 fraud cases (₹1,206 cr, nearly all already provided for) are a reminder of PSU governance and underwriting risk.

fundamental.thesis: Aster DM Healthcare runs a multi-specialty hospital chain. After merging with Quality Care India (CARE Hospitals), effective 1 July 2026, it has 38 hospitals and 10,840 beds across 27 cities, which makes it one of the larger listed Indian hospital platforms. In Q2 FY27, revenue rose 19% YoY to ₹2,829 cr and PAT rose 34% to ₹281 cr (about 10% PAT margin). Occupancy reached 68% (+335 bps) and patient volumes grew 12%. For H1 FY27, revenue was up 20% to ₹5,429 cr, normalised PAT was ₹457 cr, and EBITDA grew faster than revenue at 28%. Two cautions on these numbers. First, growth eased slightly from +20% (H1) to +19% (Q2), so the 'accelerating' label in the trend table is wrong. Second, the merger may be lifting the YoY comparisons, and we only have one clean quarter, so this is not yet a multi-quarter trend. Our sector card says hospitals compound through occupancy × average revenue per bed (ARPOB) and are capital-intensive, so we graded valuation on EV/EBITDA. At 45.9× (P87 vs the market), forward P/E of 41× and P/B of 8.9× on a ROE of just 10.1%, while the stock trades near its 52-week high (85% of range), the stock is expensive. The trailing P/E of 123× is distorted by merger exceptionals, so we did not rely on it. The biggest risk to the thesis is earnings revisions: although all 12 analysts rate it a buy, their FY EPS estimates have been cut about 18% in the last 30 days. Integration costs, ₹1,200+ cr of capex, and new hospitals that are still ramping up could push profits out further while the price already assumes a smooth merger.

fundamental.thesis: EIH runs the Oberoi and Trident luxury hotel chain, a premium hospitality franchise that benefits from the premiumisation trend and from a hotel cycle where demand is still growing faster than new room supply. In Q2 FY27, usually a seasonally soft quarter, consolidated revenue grew 16.1% YoY to ₹694 cr and owners' PAT grew about 20% to ₹136 cr, a 19.7% margin. Revenue growth has picked up from +5.0% (H1 FY26) and +7.2% (FY26) to +14.5–16.1% over the last two quarters. The Q1 PAT jump of more than 220% is mostly a base effect from last year's ₹102–110 cr Mashobra exceptional loss, and EBITDA margin of 34.3% is solid but below the 37.9% full-year FY26 level. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-heavy hotel owner. At 16.1x EV/EBITDA it trades 31% below the broad-market median (P29), and at 25.2x trailing / 20.8x forward P/E it sits far below the 60–100x the Consumer Discr. card cites for premium names. With the stock at only 11% of its 52-week range while FY-EPS estimates rose 10.4% over 90 days, I lean cheap, though only two analysts cover it and there are no tight hotel peers in the comparison set. The main fundamental risk is the heavy capex cycle: ₹393 cr in H1 left Q2 free cash flow at -₹86 cr, and finance costs nearly tripled YoY (₹15.9 cr vs ₹5.5 cr).

fundamental.thesis: Urban Company is India's largest online platform for home services such as beauty, cleaning and repairs, and it also sells its own water purifiers and smart locks (Native), runs international operations and has a Saudi joint venture. It is now funding a heavily loss-making quick home-help business called InstaHelp. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹537 cr, up 41% YoY, faster than FY26's +36%. Orders rose 103% and Net Transaction Value (NTV, the total value of services booked) rose 39% to ₹1,432 cr. Profit went the other way: consolidated adjusted EBITDA was -₹144 cr, a -26.8% margin, against +6.8% for FY26. That is because InstaHelp lost ₹174 cr, which wiped out a core business that is profitable and improving (core EBITDA ₹30 cr, up 213% YoY; India consumer margin 3.5%, up 110 bps). Since the business is pre-profit, P/E means nothing here, so I graded valuation on price-to-sales and unit economics instead. At 12.3x sales and 8.6x book value (76th percentile of the broad market), the price is reasonable for 40% growth only if InstaHelp's losses keep shrinking. InstaHelp's loss per order did improve 19% from the previous quarter but is still ₹279. I rate valuation fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that the InstaHelp cash burn continues while the newly approved ₹2,500 cr capital raise dilutes shareholders, in a risk-off market that punishes high-multiple loss-makers.

fundamental.thesis: Cyient is a mid-cap engineering-services firm with three businesses: design and engineering services (DET, about 74% of revenue), electronics contract manufacturing (DLM), and a loss-making semiconductor unit, and it recently bought TAO Digital for about ₹2,156 cr. Profit has now fallen in every reported period (-24.9% in Q3FY26, -32.3% in Q1FY27, -19.7% in H1FY27), and the semiconductor unit lost ₹58 cr at a -16.5% margin. On valuation, I used P/E and EV/EBITDA together, and the stock looks fair rather than cheap: trailing P/E of 22.6x sits at the bottom of the 22–30x IT range, and EV/EBITDA of 11.4x ranks P16 against the broad market, but ROE is only 7.8%. The low 11.9x forward P/E rests on analyst estimates that were cut 18% over the last 90 days, so it should not be trusted yet. The biggest risk is that semiconductor losses and integrating TAO keep eating into the steady DET profits, and the data has gaps: the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹1,498 cr conflicts with the filings, Q1FY27 shows two different growth rates, and the reported debt/equity and dividend-yield figures look like data errors.

fundamental.thesis: Nava is a diversified midcap that earns money from a coal-fired power plant and coal mining in Zambia (MEL), merchant and captive thermal power in India, and ferro-alloy (silico-manganese) production in Odisha. It is a power-and-metals cyclical, not a regulated utility like NTPC or POWERGRID. In Q1FY27, consolidated revenue was ₹1,212 cr, up only 1.6% YoY. PAT was ₹333 cr, down 16.6% YoY from ₹399 cr, and EBITDA fell 7.0% YoY to ₹584 cr. Revenue growth has slowed from +20.9% in Q3FY26 to +7.7% for FY26 and +1.6% now. The big QoQ jump (PAT +144%) mostly recovers from a weak Q4, helped by higher plant load factors (India 85.4%, Zambia 89.3%), and does not mark a new uptrend. Cash conversion is a real positive: operating cash flow was 2.9x PAT in FY26, with ₹505 cr of free cash flow. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA because this is a capital-intensive business. At 10.0x EV/EBITDA, 1.79x P/B and 20.9x trailing P/E, the stock sits in the bottom quartile of the broad market (P10 on EV/EBITDA, P14 on P/B), but its P/E is above the 10–18x utilities band. Once you allow for Zambia country risk and cyclical earnings, I'd call it fair rather than clearly cheap. The near-term risks are the Q2FY27 results on 12 Nov 2026, the Odisha 60MW plant shutdown in September, and the 300MW MEL Phase 2 delay to mid-2028, which pushes out the next growth step.

EV/EBITDA of 19.1× is below the 23.3× median and forward P/E of 32.9× builds in a large earnings recovery, so the grade is expensive but only with low confidence. The biggest risks are the balance sheet and dilution: debt/equity is about 2.2×, and the board has approved a fund raise of up to ₹3,000 cr, roughly 12% of the ₹24,843 cr market cap, which would dilute existing shareholders.

fundamental.thesis: Schneider Electric Infrastructure is a midcap maker of medium-voltage switchgear and electrical distribution equipment. It is positioned in India's power-transmission, data-centre, semiconductor-fab and renewables build-out, with record Q2 FY27 orders of ₹1,265 cr (+50.9% YoY) and an order backlog of ₹2,701 cr (+49.6% YoY). Revenue growth sped up from +4.8% in Q1 FY27 to +19.8% in Q2 FY27 (₹779 cr), but profit has collapsed. Q2 PAT was ₹30 cr (-43.3% YoY) at a 3.8% margin, against 8.0% a year ago. EBITDA margin fell from 13.6% to 8.4%, and H1 PAT was down 55%, because the company could not pass on copper, aluminium and steel costs fast enough and finance costs rose about 39%. We grade valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive industrials. At 76.6× (P96 vs the broad market, versus a median of 23.3×), a 146.8× trailing P/E, 55.3× forward P/E and a price at 86% of its 52-week range, the stock is clearly expensive. That price assumes the H2 margin recovery management promises, which is not yet visible. The biggest risk is that margins stay weak while analysts keep cutting earnings estimates (FY EPS -30% over 30 days, -44% over 90 days). That pattern of cuts against a still-bullish rating mix often comes before a de-rating in richly valued industrials.

fundamental.thesis: Shipping Corporation of India is India's largest state-owned shipping company, running tankers, liner, bulk carriers and offshore vessels. It is a freight-rate-driven, capital-intensive cyclical, so the Industrials order-book sector card does not really apply. H1 FY27 revenue rose 55.8% YoY to ₹4,137 cr and PAT rose 120.4% to ₹1,197 cr, faster than Q1 FY27 (+40.3% revenue, +74.9% PAT) and FY26 (+3.1% revenue). PAT margin widened to 28.9% from 20.5% a year ago, cash backed the profit (CFO/PAT 1.10x), and tankers led the growth (+62.5%, 44% PBIT margin), helped by Middle East disruption. On the yardsticks for a capital-intensive lender-funded shipper, EV/EBITDA and P/B, the stock looks cheap: P/B is 1.69x and trailing P/E is 10.65x against a broad-market median of about 35x. The live EV/EBITDA (35x), forward P/E (94x), dividend yield (424%) and debt/equity (29.45) readings look broken and were not used. My rough check puts EV/EBITDA near 5x on trailing EBITDA of about ₹3,500 cr. But these are probably peak-cycle, geopolitics-boosted earnings, and the stock is already at 66% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that tanker rates fall back as Middle East disruption eases. On top of that come stress in the LNG joint ventures (₹240 cr ILT-3 provision; auditors flag going-concern doubts at ILT-1/2/3), board committees still short of SEBI listing-rule requirements, and a government stake sale stuck since 2020.

The order book has dropped from ₹5,538 cr (H1FY26) to ₹4,675 cr (FY26), which is only 1.58x revenue, and FY26 profits converted poorly to cash (CFO/PAT 0.43x, FCF -₹344 cr). The figures implied for Q4FY26 (about ₹825 cr revenue and ₹27 cr PAT, a 3.3% margin) show margins still shrinking. Q1FY27 figures are missing and the Q2FY27 results filed on 13-Nov have not been extracted yet. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for an order-book business: at 30.0x it is 29% above the market median (P66). Trailing P/E of 69.7x is well above the 28–45x Industrials range, and P/B of 4.0x comes with ROE of only 5.8%, so the stock is expensive. The forward P/E of 28.4x already assumes the recovery management has promised. The biggest risk is that the recovery slips: management expects 60–70% of the order book to execute in FY27, plus a ₹1,000 cr BESS order book and new subsidiaries breaking even, but analysts have cut FY EPS estimates 15% over 90 days. Some live data also looks broken (69% dividend yield, a consensus target below the 52-week low), so these ratios should be read with care.

Kirloskar Oil Engines is a mid-cap maker of diesel/gas engines, gensets and industrial power equipment (B2B), with a smaller pumps/water business (B2C) and a lending arm (Arka Fincap). Consolidated revenue for H1FY27 grew 15.3% YoY to ₹4,284 cr, with B2B up 18.3%. That growth has slowed from +21.7% in FY26 (the pre-computed 'accelerating' label reads the series in reverse). Over the same period profit has gone the wrong way: PAT fell 18.9% YoY to ₹241 cr, PAT margin dropped from 8.0% to 5.6%, EBITDA margin from 18.7% to 15.5%, the lending arm's profit fell 67%, and operating cash flow turned negative (CFO/PAT -0.34x, FCF -₹296 cr) after a ₹390 cr inventory build. No order book or order-inflow data was disclosed, so the sector card's preferred yardstick can't be applied. On EV/EBITDA (22.4x, at the peer median) and trailing P/E (50.7x, above the 28–45x Industrials range and +44% vs the broad-market median), with the stock at 94% of its 52-week range, I grade it expensive: the price assumes a profit recovery the latest filings don't show yet. The biggest risk is that analysts keep cutting estimates (FY EPS -14.8% in 30 days, -18.7% in 90 days) while 6 of 7 still rate it a buy, a pattern that often comes before a de-rating. The reported 34% dividend yield is clearly a data error and was ignored. Debt/equity of 150 mostly reflects the lending book, but it still raises consolidated risk.

fundamental.thesis: Waaree Energies is India's largest solar module maker. It is integrating backward into cells, inverters, BESS and polysilicon, and it now runs India's largest retail solar distribution network, with 700+ franchises. In Q2 FY27 revenue grew +23.9% YoY to ₹7,518 cr, but growth has slowed sharply from +118.8% in Q3 FY26 to +79.2% in Q1 FY27 and +23.9% now. PAT fell -14.2% YoY to ₹754 cr as operating EBITDA margin dropped 540 bps to 17.8%. The positives are that management held its FY27 operating EBITDA guidance of ₹7,000–7,700 cr, cash conversion is strong (H1 CFO/PAT 2.1x, net cash ₹3,224 cr) and the order book of ₹59,200 cr covers 2.2x revenue. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive Industrials. At 11.3x it is about 50% below the broad-market median (P15). Trailing P/E is 19.8x (P22) and forward P/E is 15.9x, both far below Industrials norms, so the stock is optically cheap. The discount is partly earned: margins are shrinking, sell-side EPS estimates were cut about 6-7% over 90 days, and new order inflow fell to ₹7,300 cr from ₹20,500 cr. The biggest risk is a global module glut (utilisation fell to 45% from 71%) combined with US Section 232 and AD/CVD duties, which cut the overseas mix from 47% to 18.5%. Together these could keep pushing margins and the multiple lower.

RHIM (RHI Magnesita India) is one of India's leading makers of refractories, the heat-resistant linings used in furnaces, and most of its sales go to steel, cement and glass makers. The order-book KPIs on the Industrials sector card do not really fit this business, and no sector KPIs were provided. Taking H1 minus Q1, Q2 FY27 revenue was about ₹1,030 cr, roughly flat against ₹1,036 cr a year ago (-0.6%). Revenue growth has slowed from +14.3% in H1 FY26 to +5.6% in Q1 FY27 and about zero in Q2. Q2 profit after tax (PAT) rose about 63% to roughly ₹62 cr (6.0% margin), and EBITDA margin improved from about 10.7% to 12.8% at the half-year level, so the profit recovery comes from cost and margin gains, not demand. Trailing P/E is not meaningful because the FY26 goodwill write-down (about ₹556 cr; FY26 loss of about ₹382 cr) also makes ROE negative, so I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA: 17.8x is about 24% below the broad-market median (P34). Forward P/E of 20.2x (P39) and P/B of 2.1x support a 'fair' grade, and the stock sits low in its 52-week range (22%). The 3 analysts covering it all rate it buy with a ₹484 mean target, but they cut next-year EPS estimates by 10% over 90 days, and the CFO resigned on 13 Nov (effective 31 Dec), which adds caution.

fundamental.thesis: Usha Martin is a leading Indian maker of specialty wire ropes and wires. It is a niche industrial and materials business that sells into oil and gas, mining, cranes, elevators and infrastructure, with a large share of revenue from exports. Revenue growth has picked up from about +5-6% in FY26 to +14.8% in H1 FY27 (₹2,021 cr), and the implied Q2 FY27 revenue of about ₹988 cr is roughly +13% YoY. Profit growth has slowed sharply, though: Q2 PAT was ₹136 cr, up only +5.9% YoY, after +40.9% in Q1 FY27. H1 PAT margin still improved to 13.4% from 12.5% in FY26, but cash backing weakened, with CFO/PAT of 0.78x in H1 against 1.42x in FY26. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for capital-intensive businesses: at 19.4x it is about 17% below the broad-market median (P40), trailing P/E of 28.3x is at the low end of the 28-45x Industrials range, and forward P/E of 21.2x points to expected earnings growth. That makes it fair rather than cheap, especially with the stock at 77% of its 52-week range. The main risk to the thesis is that the Q2 profit slowdown is a margin peak rather than a one-quarter blip. The Q2 data is also unreliable: the filing text was badly scanned, and H1 minus Q1 PAT gives ₹129 cr against the reported ₹136 cr, which suggests standalone and consolidated figures are mixed. Several promoter-group stake-change filings (Reg 29(2)) also came in this week, and they do not say whether shares were bought or sold.

fundamental.thesis: Jubilant Pharmova is a US-focused (79% of revenue) mid-cap pharma group spanning radiopharmaceuticals, allergy immunotherapy, sterile-injectable CDMO, drug-discovery services, APIs and generics; its strongest positions are in radiopharmacy and the Ruby-Fill cardiac PET franchise. In H1 FY27, consolidated revenue rose 19.0% YoY to ₹4,599 cr with all seven segments growing (CDMO sterile injectables +33%, generics +64%), but EBITDA fell about 20% as margin dropped 550 bps to 11.3%, and PAT fell 61% to ₹87 cr (1.9% margin). The implied Q2 is weaker than Q1: about ₹31 cr PAT on about ₹2,370 cr revenue, roughly a 1.3% margin. The main cause is the loss of high-margin SPECT products while the Montreal contract manufacturing site has been shut for remediation after an FDA OAI finding. Note that the older trend rows (FY26 ₹828 cr, Q2 FY26 ₹197 cr) appear to be on a different reporting basis, so the 'accelerating revenue' signal is unreliable; the like-for-like H1 consolidated growth figure is the one to trust. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA because the business is capital-intensive: 14.2x is about 39% below the market median and P/B of 2.2x sits at P23, which looks cheap, but trailing P/E of 38.8x is at the top of the 28–40x healthcare band and ROE is only 6%. Overall that makes it fair, not cheap, because the multiples rest on depressed EBITDA, and the 19x forward P/E only holds if the H2 Montreal recovery happens. The main risk is that recovery: FY-EPS estimates were cut 25% in the last 30 days, net debt is ₹2,672 cr after an ₹800 cr NCD raise, and US tariff headlines weigh on the sector.

Deepak Fertilisers is a mid-cap maker of industrial chemicals and fertilisers. It is a leading domestic producer of nitric acid (about 60% share in concentrated nitric acid), technical ammonium nitrate (about 40%) and isopropyl alcohol (about 38% share in West India), and it also runs a weaker crop-nutrition business. In Q2 FY27, revenue rose 10.9% YoY to ₹3,334 cr and PAT rose 83.9% YoY to ₹394 cr. EBITDA margin widened 706 bps to 22.5%, driven by chemicals revenue growth of +42.5% and the Equinor gas contract. Revenue growth has eased slightly from about +12% in FY26 to +10.9%, crop-nutrition revenue fell 12.8%, and cash conversion was strong (CFO/PAT 3.3x, FCF ₹542 cr). On valuation, I used EV/EBITDA, the right measure for a capital-intensive chemicals business: 11.1x is above the 5–8x mid-cycle norm for chemical cyclicals. Trailing P/E of 16.9x sits inside the 12–22x Materials range, and forward P/E of 10.6x points to further earnings growth, so I grade it fair rather than cheap. The bottom-quintile rank against peers is against the broad market, not close industry peers, so it carries little weight. The main things to watch are whether the Dahej nitric acid and Gopalpur TAN projects (98% complete) start operating on time in Q4 FY27, and whether chemical prices hold up.

fundamental.thesis: Ramkrishna Forgings makes forged and machined parts, mainly for commercial vehicles, rail and global auto platforms, and has subsidiaries in the USA and Mexico. In H1 FY27 revenue grew 36.3% YoY to ₹2,621 cr and PAT rose to ₹117 cr from ₹2 cr, with EBITDA margin up from 14.6% to 18.1%. Revenue growth has improved quarter by quarter, from -4.5% (H1 FY26) to +19.8% (Q1 FY27) to +36.3% (H1 FY27), but much of that comes off a weak base hit by a ₹42 cr provision on bad receivables, and the yfinance quarterly figures (₹734 cr in Q2) do not match the filing-based table. Because this is a capital-intensive business, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA: 20.0x is P42 against the market and about 14% below the median, and a forward P/E of 27.7x sits at the top of the 18-28x auto-ancillary range. The 148x trailing P/E is inflated by the depressed base, so overall valuation looks fair, and with the price at the consensus target (₹697) there is little room left. The biggest weakness is cash: operating cash flow was only ₹41.5 cr in H1 (0.35x PAT) against ₹390 cr of capex, so free cash flow was -₹349 cr, inventory is building and finance costs take 4.5% of revenue. Return on equity is weak at 2.3%.

fundamental.thesis: Radico Khaitan is a premium-led Indian spirits maker whose Magic Moments brand holds about 60% of the Indian vodka market. Q2FY27 net revenue rose 16.8% YoY to Rs 1,745 cr and PAT rose 66.1% to Rs 231 cr; the table's 'decelerating' and 'contracting' signals are unreliable because it mixes revenue before and after excise duty, but on a net basis revenue growth did slow from +24.7% in FY26 while EBITDA margin improved from 16.8% to 20.4%, with Prestige & Above volumes up 35.8%, Regular & Others down 9.7%, and total volume growth (+7.2%) trailing price/mix (+9.6%). Using P/E as the main yardstick with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check, the valuation is expensive: the 81.8x trailing P/E appears to use FY26 PAT and falls to about 62x on my estimate of trailing-12-month PAT (about Rs 796 cr), near the top of the sector card's 40-65x range, while forward P/E is 51.1x, EV/EBITDA is 40.3x, broad-market ranks are P82-P93 and the stock sits at 96% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that this price needs the premium growth and roughly 20% margin guidance to hold while grain costs, state policy and higher inventory (H1 CFO/PAT 0.82x) create pressure; three snapshot fields also look unreliable, as the 15% dividend yield and 20.94 debt/equity look like unit errors and the +16.1% consensus upside does not match the roughly Rs 3,690 price implied by market cap, and the October 28 earnings call transcript is not reflected here.

E.I.D. Parry is a Murugappa-group holding company that runs its own sugar, distillery and nutraceutical businesses and holds a controlling stake in Coromandel International (fertilisers and crop protection), so consolidated numbers are mostly Coromandel's agri-inputs business, not FMCG. In Q2 FY27, consolidated revenue grew 7.2% YoY to ₹11,213 cr, but PAT fell 40.5% YoY to ₹253 cr (PAT margin 2.25% vs 4.05% a year ago). This is the third straight period of roughly 40% PAT decline (Q1 -42.5%, H1 -41.2%), revenue growth has slowed from +18-22% in FY26 to single digits, and the standalone parent lost ₹22.5 cr as the sugar segment and refinery keep losing money. The FMCG card's P/E norms don't fit a capital-intensive holding company, so I graded on EV/EBITDA plus P/B: EV/EBITDA of 5.96x (P2 among broad-market peers) and P/B of 1.53x look cheap, but trailing P/E of 29x is above the 12-22x Materials range. Domestic PV is a top-three player with about 14% EV mix and record quarterly revenue of ₹20.4K cr, but JLR luxury cars drive most of the consolidated profit. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹96,920 cr, up 33.9% YoY. That jump mostly reflects a weak base from the JLR cyber incident in Q2FY26, not real acceleration. The underlying picture is weaker: EBITDA margin fell from 9.4% in Q4FY26 to 7.4% in Q1FY27 and 5.5% in Q2FY27 on adverse mix and commodity costs. The company reported a net loss of ₹5,451 cr (-5.6% margin), driven by ₹6,738 cr of restructuring exceptionals. Before those exceptionals, profit was only about ₹1,290 cr (about 1.3% margin), and Q1 PAT was down 78.5% YoY. Because this is a capital-intensive auto maker, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA and P/B rather than P/E (trailing P/E is not meaningful with losses). It trades at 7.1x EV/EBITDA against a peer median of 18.3x and 1.29x P/B against 4.5x, the cheapest in its peer group (P0), so the grade is cheap. Part of that discount is deserved, given JLR's exposure to global cycles and tariffs, ROE of -1.1%, and interest coverage of only 1.3x. The biggest red flag is sell-side FY EPS estimates being cut 44% in 30 days, which means the forward P/E of 7.15x rests on numbers that are still falling.

fundamental.thesis: Siemens is one of India's leading electrical, automation and mobility equipment makers, with a net cash position of about ₹8,113 cr. That positions it squarely in the transmission, data-centre and rail capex cycle. In Q2FY27 revenue rose 17.0% YoY to ₹5,734 cr, accelerating from +14.6% and +14.8% in the prior two periods, and new orders jumped 37.8% to ₹6,228 cr, with the order backlog up 12% to ₹47,034 cr (roughly 2x annualised revenue). However, PAT grew only 3.9% to ₹504 cr, an 8.8% margin, and management cites commodity and foreign-exchange pressure on material costs, with operating margin falling from 11.4% to 9.5%; Q1's 45.5% PAT margin is distorted by the one-off gain on the motors-business sale and should be ignored. Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this order-book business, 52.8x is about 55% above the 34x peer median (around the 76th percentile), and trailing P/E of 76.5x sits at the top of even the 50–80x electricals band. With full-year EPS estimates cut 4.5% over 90 days, the stock looks expensive, and the biggest risk is that orders keep growing but margins don't, leaving the premium multiple to de-rate.

fundamental.thesis: ICICIPRULI (now ICICI Life Insurance) is one of India's largest private life insurers, with ₹3.29 lakh cr of assets under management, a 229.9% solvency ratio and a 99.3% claim-settlement ratio. New business has picked up after a flat FY26: in H1FY27, annualised premium equivalent (APE) grew +15.1% YoY to ₹4,935 cr (FY26 was only +2.2%), retail APE recovered from -0.1% to +9.9%, VNB grew +22.3% to ₹1,283 cr, and VNB margin widened to 26.0% from 24.7% in FY26. Gross premium grew +15.3% to ₹24,505 cr and PAT +26.5% to ₹760 cr, but PAT is not the right yardstick for a life insurer. On the life-insurer yardstick, price to embedded value (P/EV), the stock trades at about 1.24x (₹70,497 cr market cap vs ₹56,669 cr EV, which grew +12.2% YoY; FY26 return on EV was 11.9%), which looks cheap. Peer ranks agree: P25 on P/B and forward P/E, at a 22–25% discount to the peer median. The biggest risk is growth fading: management has guided that protection growth will cool from the 40–50% pace of the last four quarters, and Prudential's pending reclassification from promoter to investor could mean an overhang of stake sales, while the market is in a RISK_OFF regime.

fundamental.thesis: Vedanta is a diversified natural-resources producer (aluminium, zinc, oil & gas, iron ore, power) that sells at global commodity prices, so it is judged on its cost position and balance sheet. fundamental.thesis: Berger Paints is India's second-largest decorative paints maker, with growing industrial, construction-chemicals and international businesses; management says its market share held steady through Q2 despite the competitive shake-up caused by Birla Opus entering the market. Revenue growth has picked up from +0.4% in Q3 FY26 to +12.0% in Q1 FY27 and about +13.2% in Q2 FY27 (H1 FY27 revenue ₹6,784 cr, +12.5%; PAT ₹622 cr, +19.3%), but profitability is moving the other way: Q2 PAT, worked out from the H1 minus Q1 figures, was about ₹217 cr on ₹3,200 cr revenue (a 6.8% margin versus 11.3% in Q1), Q2 operating profit grew only 5.2%, H1 EBITDA margin fell to 14.4% from 17.0% in Q1, and H1 operating cash flow covered only 0.23x of PAT, with free cash flow at -₹82 cr. Judged the way the sector card says to judge paint companies (as consumer franchises on a 30-60x P/E band), a trailing P/E of 50.9x (38.7x forward) and EV/EBITDA of 30.9x put the stock at the upper end of fair. It ranks around P87 in the broad Materials peer set, but that set is mostly steel and metal names, and Berger still trades below its direct peers ASIANPAINT and PIDILITIND; the stock sits mid-range at 48% of its 52-week band and sell-side estimate revisions are roughly flat over the last 30 days. The biggest risk is that raw-material costs keep rising (management sees no easing, and crude is climbing) while Birla Opus competes hard, which could keep squeezing margins even as volumes grow.

Page Industries holds the exclusive India licence for Jockey and Speedo and leads branded innerwear and athleisure, with very high returns on capital (annualised ROE about 52%, ROCE about 62%) and a net-cash balance sheet of about ₹445 cr. Revenue growth has picked up over the last three quarters, from +5.6% in Q3 FY26 to +7.9% in Q1 FY27 and +11.5% in Q2 FY27 (₹1,440 cr vs ₹1,291 cr a year ago). Profit has not kept pace: PAT rose only 4.0% to ₹203 cr, because EBITDA margin fell 134 bps year on year to 20.9% and has slipped each period from 22.0% to 21.3% to 21.1% to 20.9%. Cash conversion is still excellent (H1 free cash flow ₹436 cr, CFO about 2.4x PAT). I graded valuation on peer-relative EV/EBITDA and forward P/E, the main yardsticks for a profitable branded franchise: 37.0x EV/EBITDA (P78, 69% above the 21.9x sector median) and 44.9x forward P/E (P79) put it in the expensive band, even though trailing P/E of 56.2x (P71) is only fair. fundamental.thesis: SBI Card is India's #2 credit-card issuer, a mono-line lender with about 18.5% share of cards and 18.2% of spends, earning on revolver interest and fees. In Q2FY27 revenue was Rs 5,302 cr, up 3.2% YoY, and growth has slowed steadily from +10.1% in FY26 to +7.0%, +3.4% and now +3.2%. PAT jumped 74.8% YoY to Rs 778 cr (margin 14.7%, up from 10.5% in FY26), but that came from falling credit costs off a weak base, not from growth: receivables fell 2% YoY and card spends grew only 3%, while gross NPA improved from 2.41% to 1.90% and net NPA from 1.04% to 0.77%. On the lender yardstick (price-to-book against ROE, not P/E), 3.6x book against a 14.7% trailing ROE (18.4% in the latest quarter) is fair to slightly rich: it ranks P78 on P/B and P67 on trailing P/E among credit-services peers, though the stock sits near its 52-week low, the 16.3x forward P/E is below the 26x trailing, and FY EPS estimates were raised about 7% over 30 days. The main risk is that profit growth is coming from credit-cost relief while the loan book shrinks, and that lever runs out once asset quality normalises.

Ashok Leyland is India's second-largest commercial-vehicle maker (trucks and buses), and its consolidated numbers also include its lending arm, Hinduja Leyland Finance. The latest results we have from official filings are for Q1 FY27: revenue was ₹13,070 cr (+11.6% YoY) and PAT was ₹668 cr (only +1.5% YoY), so the PAT margin fell to 5.1% from 6.8%. Wholesale volumes grew about 10% (48,763 vs 44,238 units), with domestic volumes up 12% and exports down 18%. Q2 FY27 results came out on 2026-11-14 but have not been extracted yet. yfinance shows Q2 revenue of ₹10,823 cr and PAT of ₹843 cr, but those figures are unverified and don't line up with the trend table, which also mixes period types, so the growth trend is hard to read. On valuation, I used P/E and EV/EBITDA against the Auto card's 18–30× OEM range: a trailing P/E of 23.9× is fair, and a forward P/E of 17.3× and EV/EBITDA of 10.9× point to some upside. The stock sits at 30% of its 52-week range. The peer block's 'cheapest in sector' verdict should be ignored because the peer set is mostly capital-goods names like HAL, ABB and CGPOWER, not auto makers. The biggest risk is that profit is lagging revenue while cash flow is negative (FY26 CFO/PAT -1.32x), and that comes on top of high consolidated leverage from the lending book, ahead of an RBI meeting where a rate hike could hit both truck-financing demand and the finance arm's margins.

The principal risk is that credit costs remain elevated at 2.19% and cost of borrowing continues to tick higher (7.76%, +4bps QoQ), delaying the RoA/ROE recovery the premium forward multiple demands and risking a sharp de-rating from an already near-52-week-low price.
