fundamental.thesis: India Cements is a mid-sized South India cement maker with 14.75 MT of capacity (Q1FY26). It is now controlled by UltraTech, so the story depends on a turnaround under new ownership rather than on stand-alone strength. The latest extracted figures are stale: they run only to 9MFY26 (filed Jan-2026), and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-17 have not been indexed yet. In those older numbers, cumulative revenue growth picked up from -0.2% YoY in Q1FY26 to +4.8% in H1FY26 and +10.9% in 9MFY26 (₹3,256 cr). The company was still losing money, though the loss margin narrowed from -13.0% to -3.9% (9M PAT ₹-127 cr), while EBITDA margin slipped from 9.4% (H1) to 7.5% (9M), so the fall in costs per rupee of sales has not held. Because cement is capital-intensive, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA. At 25.9× it sits well above normal cement multiples and above the broad-market median of 23.3×, and the 116× trailing P/E reflects barely positive earnings. The 1.06× P/B and the price near its 52-week low look cheap only on the surface. The 20.6× forward P/E already assumes a turnaround, while analysts have cut this year's EPS estimates by about 21% in the last 30 days. Grade: expensive. The biggest risk is that EBITDA per tonne keeps lagging the healthy ₹900–1,100 band. Rising crude-linked fuel and freight costs and a risk-off market make that more likely, and the turnaround that today's price assumes would then be pushed back.

Siemens Energy India makes power-transmission equipment (HVDC, high-voltage gear, grid stabilisation) and power-generation equipment such as turbines and services, which puts it at the centre of India's grid-capex and data-centre power build-out. Growth in the filings is strong but the data is patchy and stale: 9M FY26 revenue was ₹6,791 cr (+31.1% YoY) and PAT ₹1,128 cr (+52.2%), and Q2FY26 revenue was ₹2,394 cr (+27.4%) with PAT of ₹375 cr (+52.4%, 15.6% margin). However, EBITDA margin has slipped from 24.1% to 20.8%–22.7%, Q2 cash conversion was very weak (CFO/PAT 0.09x, FCF -₹60 cr), the power-generation order backlog is shrinking (-3.2% YoY) even as the power-transmission backlog grows (+27.6%), and the yfinance quarterly rows and the H1 figure contradict the PDF-extracted numbers. Because this is a capital-intensive order-book business, I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA: at 70.7x it is about 3x the market median of 23.3x (P95), and trailing P/E of 102.8x and forward P/E of 69.2x sit well above the 28–45x Industrials range and even above the 50–80x the sector card cites for the priciest electricals, so the stock is expensive, and at 90% of its 52-week range it is priced for perfection. The biggest near-term risk is the audited results due on 25 Nov 2026: with strong execution already priced in, any slip in margins, order inflow or cash conversion could trigger the 30–50% de-rating this sector is known for.

fundamental.thesis: Manappuram Finance is India's second-largest listed gold-loan NBFC, with 5,375 branches, 46.9 lakh customers and consolidated AUM of ₹73,303 cr, of which ₹60,640 cr is gold loans and about 17% is non-gold, mainly the Asirvad microfinance arm. Growth has sped up sharply from a weak base: Q2FY27 consolidated revenue rose 46.2% YoY to ₹3,356 cr and PAT rose 222.9% to ₹701 cr. Annualised H1FY27 ROE is 15.2% (TTM ROE is only 7.0% because of last year's microfinance losses), and forward P/E of 11.0x versus trailing 27.4x shows a strong earnings recovery is already expected. With the stock at 86% of its 52-week range, upside looks limited. The biggest risk is how much the book depends on gold prices: gold is now falling, and a sustained drop would slow AUM growth, squeeze loan-to-value headroom and could raise auction losses just as Q2 asset quality goes undisclosed.

fundamental.thesis: J.K. Cement is a mid-sized cement maker that is also building a paints business through its subsidiary JK Maxx Paints. A new ₹130 cr, 75,000 KLPA plant in Telangana is funded from a ₹600 cr paints budget. In Q1FY27, revenue grew 20.3% YoY to ₹4,032 cr, but PAT fell 15.3% YoY to ₹275 cr. EBITDA margin has slid from 19.5% (H1FY26) to 17.0% and PAT margin from 7.5% to 6.8%, so volume growth is not reaching profits. The Q2FY27 results were filed on 2026-10-24 but have not been extracted yet, and the yfinance quarterly rows (₹513 cr revenue) are clearly inconsistent with the filings and were ignored. On valuation, I used EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business: 18.8× is below the broad-market median of 23.3×, but trailing P/E of 40.8× is far above the 12–22× Materials benchmark. Forward P/E of 25.6× depends on an earnings recovery that analysts are actively cutting (FY EPS estimates down 9.3% over 90 days), so I grade it expensive, even though cement usually commands a premium and the stock sits at 13.7% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is further margin compression in a crude-up, weak-rupee, risk-off environment, made worse by spending on paints, a segment the sector card describes as structurally broken by Birla Opus's entry.

fundamental.thesis: BLS International runs outsourced visa and consular processing for foreign governments, plus a fast-growing but lower-margin digital and e-governance services arm; it does not fit the premium consumer-discretionary template in the sector card. In Q2FY27 revenue grew 32.0% YoY to ₹973 cr, up from +25.3% in Q1FY27, but PAT rose only 8.6% to ₹202 cr (Q1: +11.4%). PAT margin has contracted from 25.2% a year ago to 20.8%, and from 24.1% for FY26. The main cause is mix: digital services (H1 revenue ₹793 cr, +50% YoY) earns a 6.2% segment margin against 39.7% in visa, and acquisition costs from Atyati and the Trefeddian hotel add to the pressure. On valuation, using EV/EBITDA and P/E together with cash conversion, the stock looks cheap: trailing P/E is 13.8x and EV/EBITDA is 10.2x, both around the 11th percentile of the broad market (median 35.2x / 23.3x). It also has ₹1,665 cr net cash and CFO/PAT of 1.37x, though the price sitting at 11% of its 52-week range shows the market is pricing in a de-rating as profits grow far slower than sales. The biggest risk is that the shift toward digital services keeps diluting margins, so strong revenue growth fails to turn into earnings growth.

fundamental.thesis: CEAT is India's #4 tyre maker (global rank #4 by brand) with 51% replacement, 30% OEM, and 19% export mix, operating at 95% capacity utilisation across ~80,000 daily tyres — a capital-intensive ancillary with defensive replacement demand. Q2FY27 revenue grew a strong +26.2% YoY to ₹4,762 cr, but PAT collapsed -39.8% YoY to ₹112 cr as EBITDA margins contracted sharply from ~13–14% (FY26/Q3FY26) to just 9.5% today — this is the defining trajectory: top-line accelerating while margins are structurally compressing, driven by commodity cost headwinds from the West Asia conflict and the Camso acquisition integration costs; the DSCR of 0.84× (below the 1.0× sustainability floor) and a current ratio of 0.67× flag tightening liquidity. Valuation looks outright cheap: EV/EBITDA at 7.4× sits at P5 vs the broad market (median 23.3×), trailing P/E of 20.2× is at P23 vs peers and -43% below market median — using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive business, the stock screens as cheap, but the multiple compression is warranted given the margin collapse, and forward P/E of 15.1× implies the market expects earnings recovery, which is far from assured. The single biggest risk is that commodity costs (natural rubber, crude derivatives) persist or worsen into H2FY27, keeping EBITDA margins pinned at 9–10% and preventing the earnings recovery the forward P/E demands — a second consecutive quarter of PAT decline would trigger a meaningful derating.

fundamental.thesis: NLC India is a state-owned lignite miner and power generator. The EBITDA margin trend is down, from 37–38% to about 30.5% for FY26. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA and P/B plus ROE, as the sector card suggests for capital-intensive regulated utilities. EV/EBITDA is 9.9x, P/B is 2.1x against a 16% ROE, and trailing P/E is 12.75x, which sits inside the 10–18x utilities range. So I grade it fair, not cheap. It only looks deeply cheap against the broad market, which is not a fair comparison for a regulated power company. The main risk is heavy debt-funded capex: debt/equity is 0.82, FY26 free cash flow was -Rs 2,779 cr, and the government's newly announced offer-for-sale (OFS) adds supply pressure on the share price.

fundamental.thesis: Phoenix Mills is India's dominant organised retail mall operator (not primarily a residential developer) — its Property & Related Services segment runs ~57% EBITDA margins on a portfolio of high-footfall malls, making it closer to a retail REIT-annuity than a cycle-linked developer. Per the sector card, P/E is structurally meaningless for real estate; using EV/EBITDA (the correct yardstick for this capital-intensive model), PHOENIXLTD trades at 28.3× against a broad-market median of 23.3× (P62 rank, +21% premium) — fairly valued given the annuity-quality mall revenues, but not cheap, and the premium leaves no margin of safety against balance-sheet stress. The thesis is undermined by D/E of 37.21×, ₹2,898 cr of goodwill impairments booked in FY26, one subsidiary not on a going-concern basis, 90-day EPS estimate cuts of ~5%, and a RISK_OFF macro regime with Real Estate formally underweighted in sector tilts.

fundamental.thesis: Prestige Estates is a multi-city developer led by Bangalore, with projects in Mumbai, Pune, Hyderabad and NCR, plus a growing rental and hospitality business. It is building scale by buying land aggressively: two 100%-stake acquisitions in November 2026 and ₹2,669 cr of land spend in H1 alone. Reported H1FY27 revenue was flat at ₹4,735 cr (-0.1% YoY) and PAT fell 31.4% to ₹528 cr, an 11.2% margin. Cash conversion stayed strong (CFO/PAT 2.48x, FCF ₹323 cr). The sector card says reported P&L lags the real business by 2-4 years, and the numbers that matter most for a developer (pre-sales, collections, net debt trend) are not in the data I was given, so I can't make a confident growth call. I used EV/EBITDA plus P/B-vs-ROE because P/E is not meaningful for developers. EV/EBITDA of 21.6x sits slightly below the broad-market median of 23.3x (P46), but P/B of 4.0x against an ROE of only 8% is rich, so overall valuation is fair. The 52-week position (60% of range) and the forward P/E falling to 26.5x from 55.2x trailing look neutral to mildly supportive. The biggest worry is leverage: debt/equity is about 1.05x while the company keeps buying land, and sell-side FY EPS estimates were cut 5.8% in 30 days and 8.2% in 90 days even though 19 of 21 analysts rate it a buy. Mining brings in nearly all its revenue (FY26 mining revenue ₹2,508 cr out of ₹2,653 cr total), and the loss-making power segment adds the rest. In Q2FY27, revenue from the official filing rose 71.2% YoY to ₹903 cr, faster than +23.8% in Q1FY27. Reported PAT fell 63.3% to ₹171 cr, but that is because Q2FY26 included a one-time ₹474 cr GST credit; without it, PAT grew about 27%. The PAT margin is 18.9%, close to Q1's 18.0% and well below FY26's 36% (which was inflated by the one-off). The quarter was strongly cash-backed: operating cash flow was 3.9x PAT and free cash flow ₹376 cr. Because this is a capital-heavy commodity miner, the right measure is EV/EBITDA, and the reported 43.9x is far above the 5–8x mid-cycle norm for cyclicals. However, that figure, the 163% dividend yield and the 4.47 debt/equity do not fit with Q1 EBITDA of ₹267 cr and the low liabilities in the segment data, so I treat them as unreliable. On the more dependable cross-check, trailing P/E of 20.6x is at the top of the 12–22x Materials range and P/B of 2.78x with 14.2% ROE is not cheap. Forward P/E (22.0x) is above trailing, which means earnings are expected to fall, so the grade is fair, not cheap, even though the stock ranks low on P/E against the broad market. The biggest risk is that the 71% revenue jump does not match the yfinance figure (₹538 cr), and it brought only modest underlying profit growth while margins shrank.

fundamental.thesis: NIACL is India's largest PSU general insurer (85.44% government-owned), writing motor, health, marine, and fire coverage domestically and internationally, with a regulatory solvency ratio of 1.80×; however, the franchise is structurally loss-making at the underwriting level and profits depend entirely on investment income. Using P/B + ROE as the correct yardstick for an insurer (not P/E), P/B of 0.76× ranks NIACL at P1 in the broad peer set and appears cheap on its face, but a TTM ROE of only 3.4% fully explains this discount — it is structural cheapness, not mispricing — and analyst EPS estimates have been cut –47% in just 30 days, a classic pre-derating signal that the forward P/E of 9.2× bakes in recovery assumptions the combined-ratio trend does not yet support. The dominant near-term risk is a qualified audit conclusion on unreconciled reinsurance recoverable balances (₹75,490L gross, ₹13,783L doubtful-debt provision), compounded by a new CMD appointment in September 2026 and a mandatory Ind AS accounting transition due April 2027, leaving both governance and accounting transparency materially unresolved.

The stock trades at a trailing P/E of 80.3× and P/B of 36.78× — at P88 and P100 respectively vs the broad 499-stock market — with sell-side mean targets implying −26.8% downside and zero buy recommendations from only 2 analysts, while the 52-week position at 95.1% of range signals the stock is priced for near-perfection; using EV/EBITDA of 56.3× as the primary yardstick (per sector card for capital-light/platform-adjacent names), this is unambiguously expensive versus any reasonable comparable. The single largest risk is valuation derating from extreme multiples if AUM growth decelerates or equity markets correct, compounded by recent promoter pledge disclosures (SAST Reg 31 filings on Oct 16) which are a governance flag for a MIDCAP, thin sell-side coverage, below-1.0 CFO/PAT ratio (0.71×), and a high reported D/E of 8.25 whose nature warrants clarification.

fundamental.thesis: BSE is India's oldest stock exchange and a capital-markets infrastructure monopoly, earning revenues through transaction charges, listing fees, clearing/settlement, and investment income — it is not a traditional bank, so the relevant yardstick is P/E and EV/EBITDA (not P/B+ROE). Q1FY27 revenue grew +63.5% YoY to ₹1,566 cr and PAT grew +62.1% YoY to ₹873 cr at a 55.7% margin; while the absolute growth rate is still exceptional, the trajectory has decelerated from +116% in FY25, and PAT margins are broadly stable (55.7% vs 56.3% a year ago) rather than meaningfully expanding. At 48.1× trailing P/E (P68 vs broad peers) and EV/EBITDA of 28.4× (P63), the stock screens as fair against headline P/E metrics, but the forward P/E at 37.8× sits at P78 (expensive), P/B at 17.4× is at P94 (extremely elevated even for an asset-light exchange model), and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut sharply over the past 90 days (FY-EPS −6.6%, next-FY −9.8%) — a classic pre-derating signal that makes the 'fair' grade conditional on growth sustaining. The single biggest risk is that BSE's transaction-charge revenues are directly levered to equity market volumes and IPO activity, both of which face acute pressure from FII outflows of ₹44,000+ cr over 30 days, a RISK_OFF macro regime, and rising regulatory contribution costs (₹193 cr, +66% YoY), which could compress earnings faster than consensus currently models.

Q1FY27 revenue grew +23.2% YoY to ₹371 cr, with PAT growing faster at +31% YoY to ₹166 cr and PAT margin expanding to 44.7% — PAT consistently outpacing revenue is a quality signal of operating leverage, and EBITDA margin recovered to 64.3% in Q1FY27 after holding at 60-61% in FY26; revenue growth has re-accelerated modestly from the steady +17–18% corridor. Trailing P/E of 30× sits at P41 in the broad market (14.6% below the median of 35.2×) and EV/EBITDA of 20.87× is also below peer median — fair to leaning cheap for a 64%-EBITDA-margin business growing at 23%, and the forward P/E of 20.28× (a meaningful discount to trailing) confirms consensus expects earnings acceleration to continue. fundamental.thesis: Balrampur Chini is one of India's largest integrated sugar makers: 80,000 TCD crushing, 1,050 KLPD distillery for ethanol, 175.7 MW saleable co-generation, and a new 80,000 TPA PLA bioplastics plant. That makes it a regulated, seasonal, capital-intensive commodity business rather than a true FMCG compounder, so the FMCG sector card and its 40-65x P/E norms do not fit here. In Q2FY27 revenue grew +12.3% YoY to ₹1,876 cr and PAT rose +81.6% to ₹104 cr (5.5% margin). That rebound follows a weak Q1FY27 (+6.1% revenue, PAT -14.4%), and H1FY27 shows revenue +9.3% and PAT +38.9%, but revenue growth has slowed from the +18-22% pace of FY26 and the Q2 EBITDA margin of 9.1% is below the FY26 full-year 13.0% (seasonal, but worth watching). Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, 25.0x and a trailing P/E of 38.0x look rich against the 12-22x Materials-style range. The forward P/E of 18.5x, sell-side FY EPS estimates raised +18.7% over 30 days and +29.4% over 90 days, and a P/B of 3.4x (P38 vs the broad market) pull the overall verdict back to fair, with the stock already at 77% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is government policy on sugar export quotas, minimum sale price, and ethanol procurement pricing, together with negative free cash flow (FY26 FCF -₹349 cr) from PLA and distillery capex, which together could leave the forward earnings that justify the multiple undelivered.

fundamental.thesis: Mphasis is a mid-sized Indian IT services company with a heavy tilt toward banking and insurance clients. On valuation, I used P/E and EV/EBITDA for this asset-light IT business. Trailing P/E of 24.7x sits inside the 22–30x IT sector range and exactly at the peer median (P50). The biggest risk is that AI-led deals turn out to cannibalise legacy revenue rather than add to it, which would compress margins while the slow cash collection continues.

fundamental.thesis: Indian Energy Exchange runs India's dominant power exchange, an asset-light trading platform where most revenue (77-78%) comes from transaction fees. Revenue growth has slowed from +19.3% in Q1FY26 and +14.6% for FY26 to roughly 10-11% over the last three periods, though margins are steady to rising. Cash conversion is only moderate, with CFO/PAT of 0.73x in H1FY27 versus 0.88x in FY26. Because this is a fee-based exchange rather than a lender, I graded it on P/E and EV/EBITDA, not the bank P/B yardstick. On that basis it looks cheap: trailing P/E of 22.3x is 37% below the broad-market median of 35.2x, EV/EBITDA of 14.2x is at P24, ROE is 39%, and the stock sits at about 9% of its 52-week range. fundamental.thesis: UCO Bank is a mid-sized, government-owned lender with gross advances of ₹2,87,690 cr. Net interest income (NII) of ₹2,886 cr is about 13.9% above the year-ago revenue line of ₹2,533 cr, but that row may not be strictly NII, so treat the growth figure as approximate. For a bank we judge value on price-to-book (P/B) against return on equity (ROE), not P/E. P/B of 1.05x is cheap against the market and peers, but ROE is only 8.6% and return on assets 0.8%, well below the 12% ROE needed to call it cheap, so we grade it fair; the 12.7x trailing P/E against a 20.0x forward P/E also suggests the market expects earnings to fall. The biggest risk is funding: loans are growing about 25% while CASA (current and savings account) deposits grow only 10.6%. As a result, the CASA ratio slid from 38.65% to 36.77% and the credit-to-deposit ratio jumped from 75.5% to 82.3%. That pressures margins as the bank pays more for deposits, and it comes in a risk-off market where foreign investors are selling financials.

Hindustan Copper is India's only vertically integrated copper miner, a state-owned company whose earnings move with the global copper price. Its results have been very strong. H1 FY27 revenue was ₹2,112 cr (+71% YoY) and PAT was ₹870 cr (+174%), with EBITDA margin up to 58.4% from about 41%. Q2 on its own, worked out as H1 minus Q1, was about ₹1,176 cr revenue (around +64% YoY, slower than Q1's +81%) and about ₹518 cr PAT (around 44% margin). Earnings are also backed by cash: operating cash flow covered 0.97x of PAT and free cash flow was ₹601 cr. For a cyclical miner, EV/EBITDA is the right yardstick. At 33.4x it sits far above the 5–8x mid-cycle range for commodity Materials names, and the trailing P/E of 53.5x is above the 12–22x sector band. Even the forward P/E of 25.6x already prices in that growth continuing, so we grade it expensive despite the top-tier growth. The biggest risk is that these record margins come from the copper price, which the company cannot control. IRCTC holds the official monopoly on Indian Railways online ticketing, catering and packaged drinking water (Rail Neer), and also runs a tourism business. It has ₹3,782 cr of net cash on the H1FY27 filing. Revenue growth has sped up from +3.8% in Q1FY26 to +11.6% in FY26, then +18.1% in Q1FY27 and +17.2% for H1FY27 (₹2,703 cr), which works out to about +16% in Q2 on its own. But that growth comes from low-margin catering (+30.1%, 9.6% margin) and tourism (+21.1%), while the high-margin ticketing business (82.4% margin) grew only 0.8%. H1 profit before tax fell 11.3% to ₹798 cr, mainly because of a one-off ₹116 cr GST tribunal (GSTAT) provision in Rail Neer. Even without that provision, profit before tax was up only about 2%, so revenue growth is not turning into profit growth. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA plus peer ranks, not the 60–100x discretionary range in the sector card, because this is a government-backed monopoly utility rather than a premium consumer brand. Trailing P/E is 30.1x, at the 41st percentile of broad-market peers; forward P/E is 23.0x and EV/EBITDA is 23.4x, both near the 50th percentile; and the stock is at 10% of its 52-week range, so I grade it fair. The main risk is that analysts have cut EPS estimates about 9% over 90 days while ratings stay bullish, ticketing growth has stalled, and the January 2027 licence-fee court case is pending.

fundamental.thesis: NMDC is India's largest iron-ore miner. It is a state-owned company that sells ore at whatever price the market sets, so its profits depend mainly on ore prices and on how much it pays in royalties and levies. I worked out Q2 FY27 by subtracting Q1 from the H1 figures, because the filings do not show Q2 on its own. On that basis, Q2 revenue was about ₹6,638 cr, up about 4% YoY. Q2 PAT was about ₹1,669 cr, down about 2% YoY. For H1 FY27 as a whole, revenue grew just +2.4% to ₹13,433 cr and PAT fell -0.6% to ₹3,645 cr, a sharp slowdown from +27% revenue growth in H1 FY26 and +33% for FY26. H1 EBITDA fell 15% YoY to ₹4,712 cr, and the implied Q2 EBITDA margin dropped to roughly 23% from 46.9% in Q1, because royalties and levies grew to about 47% of revenue. I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a commodity price-taker. At 7.8x, NMDC sits at the top of the 5–8x mid-cycle range for cyclicals, which makes it fair rather than cheap. The low 10.5x trailing P/E is at the bottom of the broad market (P7), but it reflects falling EBITDA, and analysts have cut FY EPS estimates by 4.2% over 90 days. The biggest risks sit off the income statement. First, a possible Karnataka mineral tax bill of ₹16,189 cr, about 21% of the market cap, is waiting for Presidential assent and could apply retroactively. Second, NMDC is owed about ₹10,500 cr by two financially distressed steelmakers, NMDC Steel and RINL, and has provisioned only ₹651 cr against it.

fundamental.thesis: PTC Industries is a specialty investment-casting manufacturer supplying precision components to aerospace, defence, and energy sectors, having scaled consolidated revenue from ₹308cr (FY25) to ₹603cr (FY26, +95.7% YoY) on India's defence indigenisation and PLI tailwinds. Q1FY27 marks a sharp trend break: revenue declined to ₹71cr vs ₹97cr in Q1FY26 (approximately -27% YoY, reversing from +107% a year prior), PAT collapsed to ₹2cr at a 2.7% margin (vs 5.3% in Q1FY26), and the business has generated chronically negative FCF in every measured period (FY26 FCF -₹386cr, CFO/PAT -0.68×), confirming earnings are not cash-backed — EBITDA margin has also contracted sequentially from 35.2% (FY25) to 25.2% (FY26) to 18.9% (Q1FY26). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for a capital-intensive industrial, PTCIL trades at 203× EV/EBITDA (sector median 28–45×) and 259× trailing P/E, ranking at P100 (most expensive) among 473 market peers, while a P/B of 18.4× against a 7% ROE and Debt/Equity of 17.34× signals extreme valuation risk with no earnings support. Sustained EPS estimate cuts (-13.1% over 90 days, -14.6% on next-FY) while sell-side ratings stay uniformly bullish is a textbook pre-derating pattern, and any further slip in the defence order pipeline or margin recovery could catalyse a 30–50% de-rating — the historical norm for industrial cycle disappointments.

fundamental.thesis: Global Health (Medanta) runs a chain of large super-speciality hospitals across Gurugram, Lucknow, Patna, Ranchi, Noida and now Indore, with 3,811 beds. Its growth is driven by more beds and higher revenue per bed (about ₹1.46 cr per bed annualised). Revenue growth has sped up over the trend window, from +19.4% in FY26 to +26.6% in Q1 FY27 and +30.2% in H1 FY27 (₹2,773 cr). H1 PAT grew more slowly, +18.6% to ₹376 cr, and the PAT margin fell from 14.9% to 13.6% year-on-year. Part of that gap is because H1 FY26 included about ₹36 cr of one-off gains. The other drivers are a 77% jump in finance costs, employee costs up 23%, and an EBITDA margin that slipped from about 25% to 23.4%. Cash conversion is strong (CFO/PAT 1.51x), and the company reports about ₹706 cr of net cash. For a capital-intensive hospital business I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA, which is 36.2x, with trailing P/E at 61x and P/B at 8.5x. All four multiples sit around the 75th–80th percentile of the broad market and above the 28–40x healthcare P/E band, so the stock is expensive. Forward P/E of 39x and analysts raising estimates (+7% over 90 days) are already priced in. The biggest risk is that new hospitals, the Indore acquisition, the ₹997 cr Ghaziabad project and rising wages keep squeezing margins while the stock is priced for flawless delivery.

On the primary Industrials yardstick (EV/EBITDA), BHEL trades at 56.2× vs sector median 34.0× — P88 in sector, a 65% premium — and while the forward P/E of 29.7× is a reassuring P35 (below median), the stock is at 82.6% of its 52-week range with ROE of only 6.3% against P/B of 5.15×, graded expensive overall. VRS costs continued in H1FY27 (₹13 cr) along with a ₹5.8 cr forex loss, and the Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-11-03 are not yet in the extracted data. Franchisee like-for-like growth in the high single digits is the one positive KPI. I graded valuation on P/E plus ROE, because the low 13.7× EV/EBITDA is inflated by lease accounting. On that basis the stock looks expensive: trailing P/E is 75.6× (P86 vs the broad market, +115% vs the 35× median) and P/B is 6.4× on an ROE of only 8.5%. That is a premium-retailer multiple for a business growing revenue in low single digits. The forward P/E of 37× assumes a profit recovery that has not shown up yet. Sell-side views are bearish (8 sell out of 14), and FY EPS estimates have been cut 8.2% over 90 days. The biggest risk is that the margin recovery story keeps slipping while estimates keep being cut, which would push the multiple down further.

fundamental.thesis: Aarti Industries is a mid-cap Indian specialty chemicals maker (benzene-based intermediates for agrochem, pharma and polymers), a cyclical business that stands to gain from China+1 sourcing shifts. Profit is recovering from a low base: H1 FY27 PAT more than doubled (+117.5%) to ₹324 cr, and Q2 FY27 PAT of about ₹170 cr on revenue of about ₹2,631 cr puts revenue up roughly 26% YoY (vs ₹2,086 cr in Q2 FY26) and the PAT margin at about 6.5%, up from 4.7% in FY26. The revenue figures in the filings disagree with each other (the H1 total of ₹6,065 cr does not match the two quarters added together), so the reported +41% to +60% revenue growth rates are not reliable; the PAT figures do add up. Using EV/EBITDA, the yardstick for chemical cyclicals, the stock trades at 19.4x, well above the sector card's mid-cycle norm of 5–8x, and 42x trailing P/E is above the 12–22x Materials range; ROE is only 7.2% against 2.95x book, and the price sits at 80% of its 52-week range, so it looks expensive even though the forward P/E of 24x and sell-side upgrades (+5.2% over 30 days) already assume strong earnings growth.

fundamental.thesis: LIC Housing Finance is one of India's largest housing finance companies, with a loan book of Rs 3.26 lakh crore that is about 85% individual home loans, backed by the LIC parent. In Q2 FY27, revenue was Rs 7,175 cr, up only 1.4% YoY. Revenue growth has been stuck between -1.4% and +2.6% across the trend window, loan growth is just 5%, NII rose only 2% to Rs 2,088 cr, and NIM slipped to 2.58% from 2.62% (down from 2.72% for FY26). PAT still grew 11.4% to Rs 1,509 cr, a 21.0% margin, mainly because asset quality improved, with Stage 3 loans falling to 2.05% from 2.51%, rather than because the core business grew. I graded valuation on P/B plus ROE, the right yardstick for a lender: at 0.75x book with a FY26 ROE of about 14%, and at P3 of 34 Financials peers on P/B (P0 on a trailing P/E of 5.3x vs a 17.5x median), the stock is clearly cheap. The biggest risk is that 99% of the book is floating-rate, so it reprices down quickly in an easing cycle, and with growth this thin, earnings depend on low credit costs holding.

fundamental.thesis: Polycab is India's largest wires and cables maker, with about 30-31% share of the organised market. It is scaling a consumer electricals (FMEG) business and a smaller EPC arm, and has net cash of ₹4,520cr and an 11-day working-capital cycle. Revenue growth sped up from +39% YoY in Q1 FY27 to +53% in Q2 FY27 (₹9,900cr), and PAT rose 43% to ₹990cr. PAT margin edged up to 10.0% from 9.4% in FY26. FMEG grew 124% and posted its first double-digit EBIT margin (10.1%). Much of the headline growth is copper price pass-through, though: copper rose 40-45% in H1, while wire volumes grew only 10.5% and cable volumes about 5%. Underlying demand is healthy but well below the +53% headline. I graded valuation mainly on EV/EBITDA, which suits this capital-intensive business. At 35.0x it sits close to the sector peer median of 34.0x (P53). Trailing P/E is 53.8x (P50) and forward P/E is 38.5x, which points to expected earnings growth. On the sector card's 50-80x range for electricals this is fair, not cheap, and the stock is at 99.8% of its 52-week range. The main risk is that copper-inflated revenue and record margins revert as commodity prices normalise or UltraTech's entry into wires squeezes pricing. That risk is larger because, in a risk-off market, a stock priced for perfection can lose 30-50% of its valuation multiple quickly.

fundamental.thesis: Bajaj Finserv is a holding company. Its value comes mainly from its stake in Bajaj Finance, a top-tier NBFC whose loan book (AUM) grew 26% to ₹5.84L cr with gross NPA at 1.06%, plus its unlisted life and general insurers, Bajaj Housing Finance and smaller emerging businesses. In Q2FY27 consolidated total income rose 17.0% YoY to ₹43,416 cr and PAT rose 25.0% to ₹5,952 cr, a 13.7% PAT margin. Revenue growth has slowed slightly, from +19.2% in Q1 to +17.0%, while PAT growth sped up from +18.1% to +25.0%, helped by life insurance VNB rising 40% and its new-business margin widening to 21.6%. The FY26 margin of 6.5% does not line up with the quarterly figures (possibly a mix of attributable and total PAT), so the long-run margin trend is less reliable. On valuation I used P/B against ROE for the lending-heavy structure, checked against a holding-company sum-of-the-parts lens: 3.53x book for a 14.6% ROE is rich, and the stock sits at the 73rd percentile of its sector on both trailing P/E (28.2x against a 17.5x median) and P/B. Forward P/E of 18.7x implies earnings growth, and the price is only 21% of the way up its 52-week range, so overall I grade it fair rather than expensive, with no clear mispricing. The main fundamental worries are the weak general insurance arm (PAT down 19%, combined ratio 104.5%, meaning claims plus costs exceed premiums), slow retail life premium growth (5%) and analysts' earnings estimates being cut by about 3%.
